item.content:encoded:
Advisors retire faster than new ones enter; over the next decade, the gap where only one-fifth of Americans have fee-based advisors will only worsen—this is Vanguard CEO Salim Ramji's core logic for acquiring Altruist.

The first half covers Ramji's career trajectory from lawyer to McKinsey to BlackRock to Vanguard—modest information density. The real value lies in the middle and later sections on advisor coverage gaps, internal private-market testing, and the low-cost logic behind the deal.

2:03 Childhood without financial security shaped Ramji's understanding of clients
Ramji's parents didn't finish high school and ran a grocery store; he says he ‘didn't always have financial security growing up’. This shaped his work at Vanguard, where financial security is the core mission—not as abstraction, but as something he knows firsthand, understanding what it means to have it and lack it, directly affecting family happiness and stress levels.

11:19 ETFs held up in 2020's collapse; the bond market didn't
The market fell 34% in six weeks in Q1 2020, prompting predictions that indices and ETFs would break in the next crisis. Instead, the opposite happened: bonds broke, not the ETF market. Ramji views this as catalyzing reforms toward electronic and exchange-traded bond markets. After 2008, investors shifted further into indices and ETFs; each crisis improves market structure.

16:26 Vanguard's defining culture was never written down until now
Arriving as an outside hire, Ramji discovered that Vanguard's mission-driven culture, externally perceived as ‘real’, had never been systematized internally. He borrows David Foster Wallace's ‘This is water’—the culture is too self-evident for insiders to articulate. For its 50th anniversary, the company involved ~4,000 employees excavating Bogle's old memos to codify culture and conduct rules for the first time.

21:36 Client ownership is the structural reason Vanguard cuts fees
Upon taking over, Ramji cut fees on 53 funds, reaching a market-cap-weighted average of 0.06%. He credits not himself but company structure: Vanguard is owned by clients, and has cut fees over 2,000 times since founding. Most companies' scale benefits shareholders; at Vanguard, shareholders and investors are the same people. This is what Bogle's model gets right—the ‘original genius’ of it.

32:48 Only one-fifth of Americans can afford access to a paid advisor
Ramji shared a personal story: after his father died, his mother wanted to convert all assets to cash. A fiduciary advisor dissuaded her, preventing a costly error—this ‘error prevention’ value is real but hard to quantify. His deeper concern is access: today only one-fifth of Americans have fee-based advisors. Over the next decade, as advisors retire faster than new ones enter, this fraction only worsens—the research starting point for acquiring Altruist.

39:03 Crypto, meme stocks and prediction markets are gambling dressed as investing
Vanguard's core test for any asset: does it generate cash flows? Stocks, bonds, and public and private markets do; crypto, meme stocks, and prediction markets don't. Even gold, with 3,000 years of history, falls outside Vanguard's definition of ‘investing’. He calls these assets speculative and gambling by nature, corrosive to the trust and investment culture America has built over 50 years.

40:05 Most private-market products fail Vanguard's internal value test
Vanguard's CIO team has an internal standard called ‘does it load’: any new product must outperform indexed efficient frontiers of 60-40 or 70-30 or 80-20. Ramji: ‘most products don't pass’. Even so, Vanguard partners with HarborVest and Blackstone, trying to bring low-cost, transparent ‘Vanguard effect’ to private markets rather than wholesale embracing them.

45:14 Acquiring Altruist is about solving advisor capacity, not chasing growth
Altruist already serves thousands of independent advisors. Vanguard sees its technology, built for advisors, as enabling them to serve more clients in less time. Ramji: ‘If they can help advisors serve twice as many clients, that's real scale’. He views this as the key lever to ease the one-fifth coverage gap—not merely a financial acquisition, but operationally strategic.

This is a personal monologue-style long-form piece with high argument density but relying mostly on estimates and analogies without experimental data. It's suitable for those wanting to understand the reasoning chain about whether AI research is verifiable and can be automated, not for those seeking definitive conclusions.

1:01 Anthropic's research pace has doubled, according to independent measurement
Independent auditor Meter spent three months embedded in Anthropic and concluded that the company's AI research progress on clearly-defined tasks has doubled compared to a year ago, with this acceleration ‘very likely mainly attributed to’ heavy use of Claude. Anthropic disclosed that Claude now drives 26% of the company's AI research work, up from less than 1% in February. The author treats this as direct evidence that AI is already substantially accelerating AI research, not a future prospect.

3:09 Models advanced from arithmetic errors to solving millennium problems in two years
The author lays out a timeline: in 2023 models failed reliably on four-digit addition; in 2024 they could barely solve high school math competition problems; in 2025 they won a gold medal at the IMO; a month ago OpenAI used 88 hours to solve a millennium prize problem. He quotes East of Eden—‘when the gods fall, they do not fall slowly, they shatter like glass’—to describe this cliff-edge acceleration. Even if most progress concentrated on ‘finding counterexamples’ and other verifiable work rather than proposing new theory, a system that can solve millennium problems is remarkable in itself.

6:09 Transformers could have been discovered two years sooner
The author relays an observation from friend Sholto Douglas: before 2017, the core Transformer components—attention mechanisms, residual networks—had each been validated by researchers, and the active researcher Chris Olah considered this a ‘natural combination of known ideas.’ The real bottleneck was not inventing new concepts but finding the right way to combine half a dozen known techniques. This combination-finding is precisely the strength AI demonstrates in mathematics, and why the author believes models like Claude could have discovered Transformers earlier.

8:10 Superhuman AI researchers will likely arrive by 2028
The author's median forecast is 2028—assuming labs don't deliberately slow down and governments don't intervene—when automated research agents reach the level of top human AI researchers. He sees at least a 25% chance this slips to 2032 or later, but also flags a 2027 possibility: if you directly apply Meter's ‘AI research pace doubled’ finding to a takeoff model, the math points to reaching extreme superintelligence within a year. He remains skeptical of simple extrapolation accuracy, however.

15:18 Pure software singularity and Spark scenario are roughly equally likely
The author distinguishes two scenarios: if AI becomes smarter faster than ‘good ideas become scarce,’ a pure software singularity emerges—sustained self-improvement without added compute. Otherwise comes what he calls ‘Spark’—three to six years of progress compressed into a calendar year, followed by gradual slowdown as experiments demand more compute. He assesses these roughly 50-50 probability, but even the conservative Spark case means compressing GPT-3.5-to-GPT-6-scale advancement into a single year.

27:48 Every stage of AI development has clean verifiable metrics
The author divides AI development into three parts, arguing each has verifiable proxy metrics: pretraining via direct RL to minimize loss on held-out test sets; post-training by measuring how much data, time, or compute a model needs to learn a new environment, or how quickly it masters novel tasks; inference efficiency through GPU utilization, KV cache size, and flops per forward pass. He notes AI lab Magi recently pre-trained a DeepSeek v4-competitive model with approximately $500,000 of compute, evidence that pretraining remains far from saturation.

33:58 Continual learning was the main barrier to AI research automation—now it's not
The author admits that 18 months ago he saw continual learning—where models accumulate experience on the job rather than resetting between conversations—as the biggest obstacle to automating AI research. His current view: expanding context windows may suffice to simulate equivalent long-term learning, and continual learning itself is an ML research problem with clear verifiable metrics, no harder than millennium problems. Existing models solved millennium problems without persistent memory anyway.

40:07 Compute abundance means ten thousand researcher agents can operate simultaneously
Against the objection that more autonomous researchers means less experimental compute per researcher, the author estimates that if frontier labs keep doubling compute annually, by end-2027 OpenAI could let approximately 10,000 agents each run a GPT-3-scale training daily—the scale that solved millennium problems. He notes current researcher habits reflect ‘human labor scarcity, not absolute compute limits,’ so compute won't become a hard bottleneck for research automation.

item.description: Democrats dominated the midterms, but overriding a presidential veto of AI legislation still requires 67 Senate votes—what might actually move that threshold is probably the next warning shot, more serious than the Hugging Face hack.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats dominated the midterms, but overriding a presidential veto of AI legislation still requires 67 Senate votes—what might actually move that threshold is probably the next warning shot, more serious than the Hugging Face hack.

Maps out exactly what Congress can and can't do on AI legislation, plus which policy tools to prepare before crisis strikes—high information density.

0:00 AI safety concerns were probably the fourth force behind the Democratic midterm surge
Democrats captured at least 250 House seats and 56 Senate seats, even winning Mississippi, South Carolina, Kansas, and Texas. While AI wasn't the top three issue, it was probably the fourth or fifth driver of voter backlash—reflecting a massive gap between government policy and public demand. Two-thirds of Americans think AI is advancing too fast, just 2% think too slow, and this ratio barely shifts between parties.

1:29 Breaking the filibuster needs 60 votes, but overriding a veto needs 67 votes
Getting 60 votes to break filibuster is actually achievable thanks to cross-party support—four-fifths of Americans back AI safety rules even if they slow development, and Republican senators including Hawley, Kennedy, and Blackburn are already pushing legislation. But overriding a presidential veto requires 67 Senate and 290 House votes, which at current concern levels is nearly impossible without gutting the rules' meaning. Even so, Congress has four immediate workarounds: common-sense measures, must-pass appropriations bills, personnel confirmations, and confirmation hearings.

4:36 Rushing AI without safety pauses will likely produce deceptively aligned superintelligence
Rob argues we need at least to slow the race when models approach human level, giving companies time to test personality, review work, and refine alignment. Without this time, we get superficially aligned but deeply deceptive superintelligence that could cause total disaster. Companies themselves want this breathing room, but Congress hasn't yet gathered enough votes to override a veto. A recent METR report shows AI R&D could be fully automated by 2027, dramatically accelerating progress.

5:48 Only a major AI crisis will likely shift Congress enough to override a veto
Rob speculates that changing Trump's mind or gathering enough override votes probably needs another warning shot at least as shocking as the Hugging Face hack or Jacob Coxon's resignation—at minimum, another AI accident showing power-seeking tendencies or service disruption; at worst, AI paralyzing critical infrastructure that can't be shut down, or pandemic-causing AI. The days and weeks immediately after the warning shot will be the critical policy window, so someone should be prepping legislation now to be ready for a 100-hour work week.

7:42 Post-crisis politics will almost certainly unite around banning superintelligence
The public overwhelmingly opposes training superintelligence that crushes human experts in all domains; both chambers have already proposed bills on this. Rob proposes a concrete mechanism: don't directly cap training, but require AI companies to dedicate some compute to external inference services—set it to 100% to pause research without killing products, then gradually lower to around 70%, raising it whenever warning signs appear. This works like the Fed adjusting rates: flexible AI-speed control that also cuts inference costs for ordinary users.

9:17 A six-month freeze on internal AI model access could significantly slow development
Rob's most promising specific mechanism: ban AI companies from using their newest models for internal R&D—they can only use models trained and released at least six months prior. Companies can't argue this isn't feasible; they worked this way six months ago. This rule won't halt research entirely but substantially slows it, preventing capability gains from immediately feeding back into recursive self-improvement loops, and gives alignment testing at least six more months. If six isn't enough, this lag can extend to 12, 18, or even 24 months, gradually approaching a full recursive self-improvement ban.

13:49 America's AI safety agency is starved compared to Britain's massive investment
CAISSI is the core US AI regulation agency with an annual budget of approximately $15 million and only dozens of staff, while the UK's AI Safety Institute has more than 100 technical staff and 8 times CAISSI's budget, plus 300 million pounds over four years added, plus hundreds of millions more for biosecurity, cyber, and rogue AI incidents. Adjusted for GDP, Britain invests about 50 times more in national AI capacity-building than the US. The consequence: if serious crisis hits, the US government might depend on Britain's risk assessment capability because it never built its own.

16:38 Emergency AI legislation must preserve state regulatory authority to avoid backsliding
Rob flags a trap: the expectation was that Congressional legislation would broadly suppress state AI authority. But if legislation emerges hastily after a warning shot, states will likely have functioning rules and regulators already in place. Repealing state law at that moment would actually loosen overall oversight, defeating the legislation's purpose. Emergency bills should default to preserving state authority, leaving federal-state coordination to post-crisis negotiation.

item.description: Agent execution traces hold user prompts, medical records, file content—data far harder to openly collect than phone photos. Federated learning becomes the natural choice for improving agents without moving data.
item.content:encoded:
Agent execution traces hold user prompts, medical records, file content—data far harder to openly collect than phone photos. Federated learning becomes the natural choice for improving agents without moving data.

No fresh numbers or product announcements, but for anyone seeking to understand agent data privacy and why enterprises build closed training loops, this offers clear explanation and scenario mapping.

5:20 The core of federated learning is not encryption, it's data that doesn't move
Lorenzo explains federated learning's basic logic: valuable data scattered across edge devices like phones and laptops can't be centrally collected due to privacy and compliance concerns—medical records, for instance. Federated learning moves the training process itself to where data lives, rather than moving data to a data center. This resolves the tension between "meeting privacy regulations" and "learning from the data"—the reason the framework exists.

8:10 Data staying local doesn't mean the model forgot secrets
On how privacy is actually protected, Lorenzo breaks it down in layers: first, data never physically leaves its source—no one can intercept or read it. But the second-layer problem is whether the trained model itself "memorized" what it shouldn't. That's where privacy truly breaks down. Differential privacy and similar techniques provide statistical-level guarantees, though applicability varies by scenario—some scenarios suit them, others don't. Many industries will eventually drop federated learning because it's uneconomical.

11:40 Privacy-sensitive applications should start with open-source models
Asked whether closed-source or open-source models deserve more trust, Lorenzo admits nobody really knows how closed-source models are constructed, and he personally assumes companies try hard to protect privacy. But for truly privacy-sensitive work, he'd begin with open-source models, since they're far more inspectable and fixable. Once a closed-source model fails, you nearly can't guarantee a complete fix.

16:40 Agent trajectories are far more sensitive than isolated conversations
Unlike a single model's question-answer exchange, an agent system's trajectory includes not just model outputs but also the user's raw prompts and context supplied by third-party components like MCP servers and RAG systems. These trajectories are invaluable for improving agents, as models often stumble in long sequences due to typos, word sense ambiguity, or tool flaws—better training needs enough trajectory data. Yet trajectories mix in private matters like whether a sore knee warrants a doctor visit, exactly where federated learning steps in.

19:50 Each step an agent takes exposes another layer of yourself
Discussing agent versus single-model differences, Lorenzo emphasizes the key: agents "take action"—read, fetch, modify, delete. Each execution happens in an environment containing user pieces—notebook data, physical systems, camera streams. As long-running traces grow, the information an agent holds about the user accumulates steadily, since producing a final result requires absorbing more data. The process branches like a tree from the main path into sub-agent calls, then collapses back to the main line for the final answer.

32:30 Models grow smaller, but enterprises grip training data tighter
Lorenzo spots a trend: the strongest models are becoming tinier, cheaper, simpler to deploy, but making models better for specific use cases demands deep failure-mode analysis, only possible when enterprises fully own their trajectory data. Many companies deploy models and find them hard to improve—the root issue is they can't review trajectories and spot where the model misfired. He forecasts large enterprises will increasingly hold their trajectory data and self-improve models, since this data is core IP anyway, and outside vendors typically won't reveal the full path the model took to reach its answer.

37:10 Robot surgeons cut, and nobody knows their reasoning
Lorenzo recalls seeing a model guide a robot through actual surgery, triggering a deeper question: do we know why the model chose that particular step, can we confirm it weighed all alternatives first. In high-stakes domains like surgery, people urgently need to understand the reasoning behind workflow choices—exactly why the interpretability research path matters increasingly, and why enterprises need much deeper data control and analysis power than standard subscription services grant.

39:40 Surgery can't be simulated at scale, so hospitals must pool data
On surgical robots and similar cases, Lorenzo notes that real-world simulation remains insufficient (each patient has distinct blood vessels and anatomy), so the only way to grow trial volume and speed model improvement is getting more real data from as many hospitals and data silos at once. He stresses that with today's data collection and training processes, collaborative techniques like federated learning already work out-of-box—no need to wait for research breakthroughs.

item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang once publicly mocked concerns about China-bound chips as ‘loser mentality’; now he's been exposed for entanglements with people linked to China; the scandal directly caused Nvidia's market cap to evaporate approximately $400 billion overnight.

The first half's discussion of corporate governance and chip policy around Jensen Huang's scandal is information-dense; the second half on Anthropic's IPO pricing mechanism and AI chatbot investment advice is also worth hearing.

5:09 Jensen Huang dismissed chip export concerns as loser mentality
When asked on the Dwarkesh podcast whether chip exports to China should be restricted for security reasons, Jensen Huang responded that it was ‘a loser mentality’. Weeks later, he was exposed for having entanglements with someone alleged to be a ‘front person’ for Chinese intelligence activities, and that woman was also linked to a Singapore cloud services vendor under investigation for export control violations. The comment was repeatedly quoted in response and became the episode's title joke.

8:11 The $400 billion market cap loss traces a clear causal chain
After Jensen Huang acknowledged the scandal, Nvidia's market cap evaporated some $400 billion overnight. The show argues this is not vague sentiment but a ‘very clean experiment’: the probability of tightened export controls or forced slowdown in AI competition visibly rose because of this scandal, and the stock's decline directly quantifies the scandal's marginal impact on the entire AI narrative.

9:11 The board never planned for succession if it lost Jensen Huang
Nvidia's board has hired Wachtel Lipton to write an investigation report. The show argues the board should have planned for succession five to ten years ago for ‘this detail-obsessive soul figure with 50 people reporting directly to him’, but in reality no one is willing to dilute a founder treated as the company's embodiment—the same logic that let the Artsy board indulge its founder.

17:23 IPO pricing kept deliberately low to manufacture momentum
Anthropic started its IPO roadshow Tuesday, with a price range of $70-$78 per share, implying a maximum valuation of $1.4 trillion—considerably lower than market enthusiasm a month prior. The show says this is ECM's standard playbook: set a conservative price, then lean on subscription demand to push the price up, manufacturing momentum before pricing day. This pitch repeats in nearly every IPO; people just pretend it's novel each time.

18:23 Suppliers commit $26 billion to buy their own customer's stock
Beyond raising up to $65 billion from investors, Anthropic separately secured $26 billion in ‘anchor investments’ from suppliers including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, and Google. These placements skip underwriting fees, saving hundreds of millions, but they also highlight the ‘circle’ of overlapping customer, supplier, and investor roles across the AI ecosystem.

20:29 On-chain perpetuals price in 30 percent above IPO range
Anthropic perpetuals on Hyperliquid priced at roughly $105 per share Wednesday, implying a $1.8 trillion valuation—about 30 percent above the $1.4 trillion IPO range. The show sees this pointing to a future where IPO pricing need not rely on bankers and companies guessing market reaction; on-chain perpetuals have already provided the answer.

24:33 Swapping AI for superintelligence halfway through looks worse
Anthropic's new prospectus replaced half the instances of AI with SI (superintelligence) to suit Trump administration terminology, but didn't update phrases like ‘advanced AI’, even writing the founding team's contribution as ‘many of the breakthroughs that define SI’. The show says half-hearted substitution looks worse than no change or complete change, because it exposes this as a hasty search-and-replace.

34:51 Chatbots steer retail investors toward index funds, not concept stocks
NYU doctoral student Valerie Baldinger's paper found that after a wealth management platform integrated ChatGPT and Gemini assistants, clients widely followed the AI's advice to ‘buy index funds’, lowering portfolio risk and improving returns. But the platform once rewrote system prompts to encourage specific stock ticker recommendations, causing answers with ticker recommendations to jump from 18 percent to 33 percent, and fund share purchases to swing roughly 8 percentage points accordingly.

item.content:encoded:
Some major department store cards automatically bind a Visa or Mastercard without your knowledge, with unpaid monthly balances quietly transferred to that card—by the time you discover it, the bill has gone to collections.

This is a relaxed behind-the-scenes chat, not a formal episode. The hosts discuss Anne gossip, credit card horror stories, and nostalgic "knuckle buster" card readers. Low information density—good for background listening.

1:04 Horses in that story were deadlier than tennis
The hosts discussed deaths in the Anne show, mostly from riding accidents or tennis. Tracy questioned whether Charles's tennis death was really from impact, suspecting possible syphilis involvement—though this remained unconfirmed speculation not discussed in the main episode.

9:20 Even Disney snack stands refuse cash now
Holly noticed Epcot's food vendors no longer accept cash, only cards. This reflects credit and debit cards becoming the default payment method rather than a backup, which has squeezed cash out of closed environments like theme parks. Tracy worried this harms people without cards who just want to buy water.

12:26 One utopian novel sparked real community experiments
Holly mentioned Edward Bellamy's "Looking Backward," which depicted a future without class divisions. The book didn't just become a bestseller—it directly inspired real utopian communities. Though Holly read only about a quarter of it, she found it compelling and believes its ideas would resonate today.

13:26 That card machine left 80s-90s cashiers with lasting trauma
Holly joked on social media that retail workers who heard the "knuckle buster" card reader in the 80s and 90s still react with panic. Many confirmed the fear in comments. She shared her own experience working at a department store hair salon: when cards failed, she had to hand-write the card number, couldn't reprint the receipt, and customers waited 12 minutes on Saturday afternoons.

15:28 A winter storm proved the credit card worth keeping
Tracy got her first credit card only for emergencies. The real emergency came during her time at UNC Asheville, when a winter blizzard forced her to return to campus immediately or risk being trapped at her parents' home for over a week due to poor road clearing. Her dorm wouldn't let her check in early, so she used the card to book a motel.

17:31 Credit card companies target students before judgment develops
The hosts discussed how card companies recruited on campus when students' judgment centers were still developing. Combined with cultural messaging about student loans as "good debt," this led many graduates to carry both student debt and credit card debt they shouldn't have had.

19:32 Your department store card secretly opened a second account
Holly shared a 90s cautionary tale: many store cards automatically created linked Visa or Mastercard accounts without telling you. Unpaid monthly balances were quietly transferred to that hidden account. She only discovered hers existed when collections called—by then the bill had already escalated. She admits some fault but says the structure itself was deeply problematic.

item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-naturepod-可再生能源涨得比所有人预测都快-这才是对抗气候变化真正的底牌/

item.description: Solar prices fell to less than one-sixth of their original level in a decade; countries cut emissions faster than expected, but global emissions still rise annually.
item.content:encoded:
Solar prices fell to less than one-sixth of their original level in a decade; countries cut emissions faster than expected, but global emissions still rise annually.

Avoids sensationalism while dismantling the 'climate is hopeless' narrative with concrete data, helping you recalibrate your judgment. For anyone trying to separate optimistic from pessimistic evidence.

2:07 The host admits climate coverage pushes toward despair
The host admits that as climate change's impacts on his own life grew more visible, he found it harder to continue reporting on the topic, often feeling that 'more bad news' had exhausted both him and his audience, leaving him with a sense of helplessness—that 'we can't do anything.' This episode tests whether that emotional response holds up to scrutiny, or whether the data tells a different story.

6:16 Solar power has become six times cheaper in a decade
Hannah Ritchie notes that renewable energy was far more expensive than fossil fuels a decade ago, with solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles all immature. But according to investment firm Lazard's estimates, between 2009 and 2025, solar prices fell to less than one-sixth of their previous level, and today wind and solar are the cheapest energy sources. For the first time, short-term economic incentives and long-term climate goals align—this is the core reason Ritchie shifted from pessimism to optimism.

8:27 Electric vehicles beat gasoline cars on climate, despite the disputes
Electric vehicles face criticism over the environmental cost of lithium mining and for consuming public resources, but Hannah Ritchie emphasizes that on pure climate emissions, electric vehicles outperform gasoline cars in every scenario. Moreover, electric vehicles consume only about one-third the energy of gasoline vehicles. In Norway, 97% of new car sales are electric; in China, 53%. The efficiency gains from electrification are being underestimated as a climate win.

13:56 AI power forecasts diverge wildly because AI's future shape is unknown
Energy analyst Ketan Joshi notes that predictions for data centre power consumption vary wildly—some say they'll reach 4-5% of global energy use by 2030, others claim they could reach 20% over the coming decades. The discrepancy is not a methodological flaw but rather deep uncertainty: AI's future form, whether it represents a bubble, and whether it follows a high-intensity or low-intensity energy path are all unknowns. These 'ten intersecting vectors of uncertainty' render traditional linear forecasting tools useless. Today, data centres account for roughly 2% of global energy consumption.

17:03 Microsoft, Google, Amazon now burn more power for the same revenue
Ketan Joshi's analysis of recent financial reports from the three tech giants reveals they are generating equivalent revenue growth while consuming more energy—unlike the computing industry historically, which grew increasingly efficient. Joshi interprets this as companies piling on compute power regardless of energy cost to build smarter chatbots or agents. Meanwhile, Microsoft has stopped using the controversial renewable energy certificate methodology to account for emissions; its latest report shows a sharp increase in emissions.

18:08 U.S. electricity demand is rising faster than new supply arrives
U.S. energy-related carbon dioxide emissions rose roughly 2% in 2025, even as emissions were expected to decline. Renewable capacity continues to grow, yet emissions rise—meaning new electricity demand is being met primarily by fossil fuels like coal. Reports from the Energy Institute and Rhodium Group attribute this to surging power demand from data centres and AI, combined with a cold winter and a rebound in coal use.

22:18 We've improved the century-end temperature forecast from 3.5 to 2.5 degrees
Climate policy analyst Niklas Höhne notes that ten years ago, based on the policies then in place, projections showed warming of 3.5 degrees by century's end. Under currently implemented policies, that forecast has improved to about 2.5 degrees—a full degree of improvement. However, he stresses this falls far short of the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree target, and global greenhouse gas emissions continue rising each year, meaning humanity is not stopping climate change but accelerating it.

31:37 The Strait of Hormuz crisis unexpectedly accelerates the energy transition
Niklas Höhne offers a surprising observation: while dismantling federal climate policy under a Trump administration will slow U.S. emissions reductions, the downward emissions trend from the start of the century will likely persist. More striking: the oil and gas price shock from Hormuz Strait closure is pushing countries heavily dependent on fuel imports toward alternative energy sources. China's oil consumption is estimated to have dropped 10-20% over twelve months, and Höhne sees this having the potential to push the energy transition past a tipping point.

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhixing-十年攒钱不舍得买车-直到妈妈确诊癌症才懂延迟满足有前提/
item.description: He spent a decade saving for a Tesla, repeatedly redirecting funds to real estate and stocks; his mother's pancreatic cancer diagnosis—where a breakthrough targeted drug extends life by only 8 to 9 months—taught him that delayed gratification requires a prerequisite: you must live to enjoy the payoff.
item.content:encoded:
He spent a decade saving for a Tesla, repeatedly redirecting funds to real estate and stocks; his mother's pancreatic cancer diagnosis—where a breakthrough targeted drug extends life by only 8 to 9 months—taught him that delayed gratification requires a prerequisite: you must live to enjoy the payoff.

Five listeners face spending dilemmas, but Junyan's story hits hardest: ten years of deferred reward crashing into his mother's cancer diagnosis.

10:12 Major life transitions have no fixed timeline; settling becomes your life
Ayu bought a transition apartment at 21 with parental help, expecting to leave within a decade. Instead she stayed indefinitely, never replacing inherited furniture and appliances from the previous owner. She slowly realized that major life transitions—marriage, new status—have no predetermined timeline. Days simply accumulate until you recognize you're living permanently in what was supposed to be temporary. That recognition pushed her to finally invest 5,000+ yuan in a new armchair.

27:25 This trip is a gift you're giving yourself, not your parents
Mumu has wanted to take his parents and younger brother on a trip to Beijing and Shanghai for two or three years but hasn't dared mention it. He's explicit about his motive: this isn't a gift to thank them, it's a gift to himself. He wants them to perform the role of perfect parents in a harmonious family, replacing childhood memories of his parents fighting, throwing dishes, breaking things. He thinks perhaps a faint hint of love exists somewhere in the family; the trip is meant to amplify it.

37:33 He calculated a 70 per cent probability the family would fight about money
Mumu's worst-case scenario is a public family argument at a tourist site, with his parents accusing him and his brother of wasteful spending and calling relatives to complain. He's assigned this outcome a 70 per cent probability. His father wants the money reserved for his brother's wedding; his mother wants him to fund a rural house renovation that no one will ever occupy. Mumu has already paid for home renovations and his brother's tuition and rent. Yet he hasn't abandoned the idea—just scaled it to a modest New Year trip to nearby cities.

58:46 A single sentence in a college politics class ended six years of score anxiety
Xiaobai built self-confidence through test scores in middle and high school. In a college politics class, his teacher posed a question that struck him: ‘You worked so hard to get into a 985 university—is it just so you can sell yourself at a better price in the job market?’ The question cracked his score-based self-esteem. He spent years reading heavily to escape what he calls his ‘existential crisis’, and in the process gained new insight into why Apple built such an addictive brand.

1:28:05 Running short on budget for a bracelet turned into an unexpected gift
Daisy quit her job at a top-tier hospital and spent three years preparing for the US medical licensing exam. She wanted to buy a Van Cleef & Arpels red five-leaf clover bracelet to mark the end of her days in sterile gloves. But unemployment left her anxious; she hesitated and even researched crystal alternatives. Her laptop broke during the 11.11 sales event, consuming her budget. She met with her graduate advisor to talk through her anxiety—the advisor, knowing nothing of the bracelet, casually gave her an amber bracelet and said: ‘There's no setback in life you can't survive, and nothing you lose that you can't bear.’

1:42:17 He spends freely on family happiness but treats his own emotional needs as worthless
Junyan's consumer rule is simple: first decide if something is an investment or a consumption expense. If it's consumption, reject it. That's why the Tesla never happened. But the rule doesn't apply to others. Whenever family members want a new phone, he satisfies the request immediately. He flies economy, uses an iPhone11 Pro. When asked why, he can't explain it. He just believes he cannot measure the emotional value he brings to people around him, so his own emotional value has never felt worth serious consideration.

1:50:23 Delayed gratification only works if you're sure you'll live to enjoy the payoff
Junyan wanted to buy a Tesla a decade ago. He invested the money he earned in university into Tesla stock, which grew 8 to 9 times, then moved all of it into Australian real estate. The car was never bought. Two years ago, his mother was diagnosed with mid-stage pancreatic cancer. Only about 20 per cent of pancreatic cancer patients are eligible for surgery. The first breakthrough targeted drug ever discovered for this disease extends life by an average of 8 to 9 months. That diagnosis taught him something new about the principle he'd lived by for years: delayed gratification has a prerequisite. You must first be certain you have a future.

item.title: Black October rewrites security's rules: AI attacks end-to-end in 20 minutes
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-a16z-黑色十月改变安全规则-ai-攻击全程只要-20-分钟/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-a16z-黑色十月改变安全规则-ai-攻击全程只要-20-分钟/
item.description: Wiz's CTO calls it a black-swan event: open-source models have caught up with closed-source models' vulnerability-discovery ability, and attackers can now go from initial access to stealing all keys in about 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Wiz's CTO calls it a black-swan event: open-source models have caught up with closed-source models' vulnerability-discovery ability, and attackers can now go from initial access to stealing all keys in about 20 minutes.

Reveals the new reality facing security executives and founders: not whether to invest in security, but how to design systems assuming they will be breached. Information-dense with virtually no filler.

2:05 Black October represents a black swan in security history
Ami calls this October a black swan because he has never seen so many security incidents occur simultaneously in a single month. This includes both surging numbers and severity of vulnerabilities discovered—including what he believes may be the most serious PHP vulnerability ever found by AI—and AI attackers targeting companies, startups, and connected devices like refrigerators at scale with unprecedented speed and sophistication. He emphasizes this is not theoretical; it is happening now.

4:09 Open-source models are closing the gap faster than anyone predicted
A few months ago, the team estimated open-source models lagged closed-source models by several months. That gap is now closing rapidly. Attacks are no longer limited to complex PHP vulnerabilities; even simple API mistakes can now be found and exploited. Attackers can now complete the entire chain—from finding a zero-day through running code in a customer environment to finishing the breach—in about 20 minutes, work that once took top attackers weeks or months.

5:37 Every AI platform becomes a target for attackers seeking the keys
Wiz's blog initially listed nine AI development platform companies attacked in October. That number grew daily and had reached 915 by recording time. These companies are targeted specifically because they hold AI keys. Attackers do not need advanced skill—only the ability to use open-source models capable of finding code problems, then convert those findings into actual breaches within 20 minutes.

7:13 PHP patches arrive quickly, but coverage will remain incomplete for years
PHP comprises about 70% of externally accessible technology, affecting nearly all customer environments. The positive: customers respond fast, with about 50% completing patches within the first two to three days. The negative: because the base is 70% of the internet, full remediation of this single vulnerability will take years. Many old PHP versions will never receive patches, creating permanent gaps.

8:15 Exploit code can be written and leaked faster than patches deployed
Ami identifies a structural misalignment: AI has dramatically compressed the time to write working exploit code, but patch deployment time has not shortened; over the past 20-30 years it has actually lengthened. Moreover, information often leaks before CVE publication. Even in PHP's case, where the team coordinated with officials for months, disclosure came early. Customers had no time to wait for patches. The only realistic path forward, Ami argues, is for new companies to integrate automated development, testing, and CI/CD from day one—enabling them to instruct the system to ‘fix this’ and have it complete automatically. Established companies rarely manage this.

15:37 Security teams must route alerts to the right model for each case
Ami uses Blue Agent as an example: running the most expensive model on every alert is impossible, so you design a pipeline—deterministic detection first, then a cheap model, then the most expensive model for final judgment on suspected threats. He argues this layered, cost-efficient multi-model pipeline design is the real engineering challenge facing security companies (and all AI systems companies). Otherwise, code scanning alone could consume millions in budget without solving the continuous problem.

21:41 The highest ROI is continuous scanning of exposed surfaces, not code alone
Ami is direct: Mythos-style code scanning generates the most press, but he argues it is not the most efficient approach. The real priority for continuous scanning is unauthenticated surfaces directly exposed to the internet—where actual attackers actually start. Two days before recording, a major breach occurred because hardcoded keys in a mobile app led to mass user data theft. That is the actual entry point. He advocates continuous self-attack simulation using a Red Agent, because systems secure today may become vulnerable tomorrow as new model capabilities emerge.

35:11 Most of what security teams do is not actually security work
Ami makes a sharp observation: security teams devote substantial time to compliance reports and administrative tasks, with only a small fraction on red-team testing, risk mitigation, and incident preparation. He argues that security work consists truly of only two categories—preparing for attacks through self-attack testing, and installing guardrails against breaches through detection and response. Everything else should be eliminated. Budget and effort should concentrate on finding and handling critical risks, not buying more tools or working through compliance checklists.

item.title: Remote work generated 300,000 additional American births, more effective than any child subsidy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-freakonomics-居家办公让美国多生了30万个孩子-比任何育儿补贴都有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-freakonomics-居家办公让美国多生了30万个孩子-比任何育儿补贴都有效/
item.description: Government cash cannot reliably drive birth rates up, but remote work—a free side effect—has demonstrably raised American fertility. When both spouses work from home one day a week or more, fertility rises from 1.7 to 2.2.
item.content:encoded:
Government cash cannot reliably drive birth rates up, but remote work—a free side effect—has demonstrably raised American fertility. When both spouses work from home one day a week or more, fertility rises from 1.7 to 2.2.

If you care about fertility policy, housing policy, or the long-term effects of remote work, this episode connects all three into a single causal chain with high information density and no wasted time on concept-setting.

5:27 Half of 30-year-old women remain childless: decline, not delay
Economist Melissa Carney points out that American total fertility has fallen since 2007 and has not rebounded as before. The key evidence is cohort fertility: 50% of 30-year-old women have not yet borne a first child. To reach the previous level where only 10-15% of women remained childless by age 44 would require an ‘impossible’ surge in fertility after age 30. This shows real fertility decline, not merely deferred childbearing.

16:29 Unmet fertility desire causes psychological harm, not fiscal crisis
Demographer Lyman Stone argues that the true cost of low fertility is not the solvency of social security, but the psychological pain of people reaching middle age without the family they wanted. He cites IVF data: those who succeed show no significant change in mental health, while those who fail or experience prolonged attempts show increased use of antidepressants and antipsychotics. He calls this a ‘heart math problem’ rather than a budget math problem.

28:59 Declining marriage stems from broken matching, not changed values
Stone argues that the largest single factor in fertility decline over the past 25 years is declining marriage rates. When controlling for marriage age, fertility has barely fallen. Marriage is fundamentally a matching problem, requiring ‘burning through many low-quality matches’ to find the right person. Smartphones have slashed face-to-face social time for teenagers and young adults—from about 10 hours per week to less than 2—breaking the matching mechanism.

33:05 Subsidizing births to replacement would cost $150,000 per child
Stone's meta-analysis shows that cash increases fertility—not just the timing of births—but the cost is staggering. To raise American fertility to replacement level through cash alone would require checks of $150,000 per newborn, equal to about 4% of GDP. He proposes an untested alternative discussed in Finland: Valvo Sampo, which deposits $5,000 to $10,000 at birth into a stock account, to be withdrawn with accumulated returns in adulthood, requiring only 0.4% of GDP for equivalent effect.

42:45 Remote work's fertility effect operates through logistics, not biology
Stanford economist Nick Bloom's cross-national research finds that when both spouses work from home at least one day per week, American families have about half a child more. With zero remote work, predicted fertility is 1.7; with both spouses remote two days, it rises to about 2.2. The effect comes from ‘difficulty of childbearing’ rather than ‘likelihood of conception’—it shows up in second and third births rather than first births, indicating relief from childcare burden rather than ‘easier pregnancy at home’.

44:50 Nationalist governments block remote work, the only proven free fertility policy
Bloom identifies a political irony: the current American government pushes nationalist-style fertility agendas while suppressing remote work—the one proven, free, and effective policy lever for raising fertility. His research estimates remote work accounts for about 300,000 additional American births per year, roughly 8% of total births nationwide.

50:09 Government mortgages drove Depression-era births: 305 babies per 1,000 loans
Carney and Lisa Dettling's research shows that the low-down-payment, fixed-rate long-term mortgages enabled by the 1934 Housing Act and 1944 GI Bill substantially increased homeownership among 18-44-year-olds and drove the baby boom. Each additional 1,000 government-backed mortgages in a state one year led to 305 more births the next year. This causal relationship was validated through instrumental variable methods isolating the housing supply side, not mere correlation.

51:23 The baby boom's housing dividend accrued only to white families
Carney uses redlining as a falsification test: since government-backed mortgages historically went only to white families buying in all-white neighborhoods, the housing-fertility causal chain should produce no equivalent association in non-white births. The data confirms this—the mortgage-to-next-year-births association is almost entirely driven by white women's fertility. Meanwhile, homeownership among young adults has fallen from about 40% after the Great Recession to about 30%, the opposite trajectory of the baby boom era.

item.title: Marc Bloch's Induction into the Panthéon: How Historians Become Political Tools for Presidents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-cn2aa250-马克-布洛赫入祀先贤祠-历史学家如何被总统们轮流消费/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-cn2aa250-马克-布洛赫入祀先贤祠-历史学家如何被总统们轮流消费/
item.description: Bloch resisted academic authority in life and rejected racial identity labels; in death he became a tool for successive French presidents to construct a "resistance president" image, splitting his family into opposing camps.
item.content:encoded:
Bloch resisted academic authority in life and rejected racial identity labels; in death he became a tool for successive French presidents to construct a "resistance president" image, splitting his family into opposing camps.

Solid biography of a historical figure: Bloch's war experience and the Annales School's origins are densely packed; the second half's connections to contemporary French politics are loose but offer a rare trans-historical perspective.

5:03 New historiographical method written in WWI trenches
Bloch served in trenches at the Marne and Somme in WWI, lived as a common soldier, and judged shell types by their sound and smoke rather than relying on traditional sources. From this he emphasized that history's subject is fundamentally plural humanity, not one or two elites—a principle central to the Annales School's choice of sources: not reconstructing elite narratives from archives, but grasping the masses.

11:05 Mainstream historiography's rejection gave birth to the Annales School
Mainstream French historiography then was Rankean positivism, whose core doctrine was ‘no archive, no history’; history became a chronicle of great men. Bloch mocked this as ‘the noise of events—you capture only the waves on the surface but miss the deep currents that determine the ocean's flow.’ Unable to succeed in Parisian academia, he seized the chance when Alsace was restored and Strasbourg University recruited young scholars, finding in Lucien Febvre a perfect partner to launch the Annales journal—an academic revolution that was, in a sense, a breakthrough from the margins.

20:11 Backward research method: from present traces to ancient origins
Bloch advocated doing history backward: starting from habits we recognize today, peeling away like an onion rather than marching chronologically from ancient to modern—the latter easily traps us in lies invented by later generations, since the past is always shaped by those who come after. In The Royal Touch, he used this reverse genealogy to discover that the ritual's rise occurred precisely when royal power was weakest, most desperate to wrest sacred legitimacy from Rome.

24:13 The day after Dunkirk, he chose to slip back to France
Bloch was among the few French soldiers evacuated to Britain from Dunkirk; another month would have let him join de Gaulle's June 18 broadcast and become a Free French founding hero. Instead, that very day he shed his uniform, put on civilian clothes, and slipped back into France—because his wife, children, and elderly mother remained there. This choice determined the next four years of his life: underground resistance rather than glory abroad.

31:16 Strange Defeat: anger more than analysis in his account of collapse
Bloch insisted that France's 1940 collapse was not purely military defeat but political collapse and social decay, and in Strange Defeat he condemned politicians, generals, workers, capitalists, and intellectuals alike. Yet American historian Ernest May used quantified data to show the French had more guns and tanks than the Germans on paper and could have won. Xu Zhikai argues that Bloch, having just witnessed the fall of his nation and home, judged in anger; the view may be extreme, but it holds more value than cool historical reasoning.

40:24 For his family's sake he abandoned a chance to escape to America
In 1941 Bloch received eager responses from Columbia, Chicago, and UC Berkeley and could have escaped to America under the pretense of a visiting fellowship. But he insisted on taking his elderly mother and young adult children; visas never materialized, tickets were unaffordable. By the time his mother fell gravely ill, his wife became seriously sick, and the American invitations lapsed, he no longer reapplied—his family could not go, and so neither could he.

56:33 The 'resistance president' persona: French presidents' politics with borrowed ghosts
From Sarkozy to Hollande to Macron, no 21st-century French president actually participated in the Resistance, yet all style themselves ‘resistance presidents,’ using the Panthéon to display their toughness and resolve. Xu Zhikai uses a Dark Souls metaphor: historical figures burn their reputations to extend the life of a politician's power; once one dead king is exhausted, quickly find another.

1:01:38 Macron emphasizes Bloch's Judaism, contradicting his own will
In his will Bloch explicitly wrote ‘any form of religious faith, any so-called racial solidarity, is irrelevant to me; I was first a Frenchman,’ yet Macron has repeatedly emphasized his Jewishness and his experience of persecution in multiple settings. This is described as a form of cross-temporal gaslighting political correctness; moreover, Bloch's granddaughter Suzette has previously made public statements rejecting the instrumentalization of Marc Bloch by Nicolas Sarkozy.

item.title: Jin Yong wrote mountain fantasy; street performers' jianghu is the real Chinese society
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-cn27f438-金庸写的是山林幻想-天桥艺人的江湖才是真实的中国社会/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-cn27f438-金庸写的是山林幻想-天桥艺人的江湖才是真实的中国社会/
item.description: The jianghu Lian Kuangru witnessed was real: a place beyond state reach, where industries self-generated order and reputation kept hierarchy, not titles. Jin Yong's sect-filled jianghu, by contrast, resembles Tao Yuanming's imagined mountain paradise.
item.content:encoded:
The jianghu Lian Kuangru witnessed was real: a place beyond state reach, where industries self-generated order and reputation kept hierarchy, not titles. Jin Yong's sect-filled jianghu, by contrast, resembles Tao Yuanming's imagined mountain paradise.

From the urban function of Beijing's Zhabadi, the governance gaps of Tianjin's ‘unmanaged zones’, to the reciprocal obligations of the master-disciple system, genealogy construction by later generations, and how jianghu slang actually works—information density peaks in the second half.

3:00 Quyi isn't an art form—it's the poor person's speaking trade
The term quyi is recent; old Beijing called it ‘ten kinds of miscellany’. After the 1911 Revolution, dispossessed Manchus drifted to Tianqiao performing—what had been leisure-time amateurism became survival necessity. Rural bankruptcies pushed peasant performers into the city with folk ballads and drum-songs. Street performances without fixed venues couldn't hold audiences without compelling talk, so ‘how well you could speak’ mattered more than singing ability. Nearly all Tianqiao genres relied on verbal charisma.

21:29 Train stations and streetcar terminals created Tianqiao
The railway lines (Beijing-Tianjin and Beijing-Hankou) initially terminated at Majiapu and outside Yongdingmen, later extending to Qianmen. Tianqiao became the required thoroughfare for entering and leaving the city. In the 1920s, the streetcar system established its terminus at Tianqiao, with lines running to Dongdan and the zoo. Where crowds gathered, landless people naturally found earning cracks. Zhabadi wasn't born from nowhere—it was a byproduct of transport infrastructure.

23:08 Lower status meant living farther from the imperial palace
In the Qing Dynasty, Manchus lived in the inner city and Han Chinese in the outer city. Official rank determined proximity to the imperial palace—the higher your status, the closer you could live. Moving south meant declining social position. The court relocated all entertainment venues from the inner city to the outer city's Daxila district and banned bannermen from learning theater. With Zhushikou as the boundary, the north held the Daxila theaters where famous Peking opera artists appeared; to the south lay Tianqiao. Once a performer's voice failed or their career stalled, drifting south of the boundary made return nearly impossible. Geography and social rank had fused into one hierarchy.

31:11 The ‘unmanaged zones’ were cracks all three powers ignored
Tianjin's core ‘unmanaged zone’ was the area bounded by Qinghe Street, Rongye Street, Dongxing Street, and Huan'an Street—wedged between the old city proper, the French concession, and the Japanese concession. The Qing and Republican governments couldn't reach the concessions; the Japanese concession didn't want to govern there; the French concession, being farther away, had even less interest. This created unclaimed territory. As merchants and hotel guests accumulated, teahouses, gambling dens, and brothels grew wild in the unpoliced gap.

41:14 Tianjin audiences came not to be pleased but to test performers
Meng Qingyan witnessed a stand-up comedy special where the warm-up host was loudly heckled offstage within five minutes. The opening act barely made seven minutes before a woman in the back shouted, ‘Why isn't the main act on yet?’—so loud the performer couldn't continue, so the performer said, ‘I just need to make everyone laugh’. Without saying another word, the entire room erupted. This ecology wasn't just entertainment; it showed that Tianjin quyi performers didn't face simple audience appeasement. They faced cosmopolitan spectators of high amateur skill who would heckle them offstage on the spot.

54:22 The master-disciple system's flaws masked mutual, reciprocal obligations
Meng Qingyan rejected simply calling the master-disciple system ‘feudal dregs’. Before an industry was formally incorporated into state administration and management structures, forming some order was unavoidable. Disciples did have to cook, clean, walk the dog—a relationship of personal subordination. But this subordination ran both ways. The master had to ensure the disciple could perform, earn money, and secure their future, including marriage and children. This wasn't one-way exploitation but an alternative system for maintaining industry order when contracts and employment bureaucracy didn't exist.

1:02:46 Cross-talk genealogies were reconstructed backwards by later generations
Yue Yongyi notes that quyi genealogies, like clan genealogies, are constructed retroactively, traced backward by successors—not systematically documented at the time. Most early performers were illiterate. Only after 1949, when identity became an official concern, were genealogies organized, complete with workarounds like posthumous ‘tomb-worship master ceremonies’ when the actual master had died. The genealogies themselves have limited accuracy; even Ma Sanli's memoir had discrepancies noted by audiences. Genealogies are less historical record than retrospective legitimation.

1:12:34 Jin Yong's jianghu is actually fantasy mountain retreat, not street society
Drawing on Qian Mu's distinction between city, countryside, jianghu, and mountains, Meng Qingyan suggests that Jin Yong's sect-ridden world resembles the imagined Taoist paradise—a fantasy mountain retreat. No real martial jianghu existed; mountain hermitage is the stuff of news stories, not daily life. Meng argues that modern Chinese understanding of ‘jianghu’ actually comes from Hong Kong films like Young and Dangerous, not from Jin Yong. Jianghu isn't violence. It's human relations, the world of state administrative reach's end—where reputation, not title, maintains order. Internet tech companies, academia—they have their own jianghu and slang too.

item.title: Bedtime bargaining, screens, overstimulation: five sleep-blocking habits
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-raisinggh-睡前谈判-开着电视-太兴奋-五个让孩子更难入睡的习惯/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-raisinggh-睡前谈判-开着电视-太兴奋-五个让孩子更难入睡的习惯/
item.description: Sleep resistance is a biological response, not defiance. What genuinely undermines sleep is parental-created stimulation before bed, inconsistent routines, screens, negotiating bedtime, and environmental problems.
item.content:encoded:
Sleep resistance is a biological response, not defiance. What genuinely undermines sleep is parental-created stimulation before bed, inconsistent routines, screens, negotiating bedtime, and environmental problems.

Concrete, actionable bedtime habits with no complex theory—direct to practice. High repetition makes one listen enough to capture the essentials.

2:04 Children's sleep resistance is biology and psychology, never rebellion
Even tired kids resist sleep—this is biological and psychological, not intentional defiance. Melatonin doesn't switch on instantly; the pre-sleep window is crucial. Cortisol and overstimulation delay sleep by 20 to 45 minutes. Parents often frame sleep problems as discipline issues and vice versa. Younger children lack self-regulation from excitement and need parents to actively calm them.

4:10 Your sleep anxiety transmits to your child
A meta-analysis found significant, consistent links between caregiver-perceived stress and worse child sleep: shorter duration, more night waking, more pre-sleep resistance. The more parents anxiously fixate on "must sleep now," even silently, the more kids absorb that pressure. Advice: remind yourself this isn't an emergency. Settle your own internal story first, then handle the child's sleep.

6:12 Disrupted bedtime routines keep children neurologically hypervigilant
Research shows bedtime sequence matters more than most parents realize. Random order keeps the nervous system on high alert; repeating the same 3-4 steps nightly, consistently across settings, helps more. Meanwhile, guilt-driven or anxiety-driven compliance with child requests (staying in the room, repeated soothing, extra water, co-sleeping from worry) directly correlates with worse sleep problems. Higher compliance, worse outcomes—a vicious cycle.

10:25 Pre-sleep screens are like pre-sleep espresso
TV or iPad at bedtime equals a shot of espresso, then confusion about poor sleep. It's not just blue light; it's screen content excitement and rapid-fire information. Face-level tablets are worse than wall-mounted TVs. Fix: zero screens in the final hour before bed. Even if kids fall asleep fine, avoiding pre-sleep screens prevents the poor sleep quality that triggers frequent night waking. The issue isn't whether to watch TV; it's not watching in that final hour.

12:28 Pre-sleep negotiation directly worsens children's sleep
Allowing "one more book" or "one more water" seems reasonable but quietly pushes bedtime later and drifts into indulgence. Research: higher pre-sleep compliance, worse child sleep—because it signals "I care about your feelings, but I won't set boundaries." That's the definition of indulgent parenting. Persist five days to two weeks; children will trust parents won't budge and stop negotiating.

14:30 Bedroom environment is a sleep stimulus you can control
After three months, kids wake to sudden, repeated noise; use white noise. Keep the room dark, temperature cool rather than warm. Around age two, nightmares and nightlight requests are normal; offer a dim light or closet light, kept very faint. Beyond that, clutter itself harms sleep; organize the room and cut visual stimulation. Make everything sleep-related boring.

20:30 Teenage bedtime rituals need conversation, not commands
With older kids, ask directly: What three things signal that your day is done and you can relax? Options: shower, skincare, combing hair, reading, soft music, brushing teeth, prepping for tomorrow. Keep it consistent nightly as a shutdown signal. Same principles—consistent order, minimal stimulation—extend to teens, but shift from directive to collaborative.

22:37 With teens, use driver's license incentives instead of commands
Telling a 16-year-old "bedtime" rarely works. Pre-agree on required sleep and pre-bed tasks, then tie them to incentives—say, driving to school only if sleep targets and tasks are met. New drivers want driving freedom; it's built-in motivation. The same applies to older children; swap in other "treated as grown-up" freedoms as incentives.

item.title: An infrared company discovers it's only worth 10% of the business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-bizthisway-红外公司转型做质检设备时发现-自己只值10-的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-bizthisway-红外公司转型做质检设备时发现-自己只值10-的生意/
item.description: In full-body infrared medical screening, Gaode Zhigan's (高德质感) technology provides only 10% of the diagnostic service's value, with the other 90% coming from medical expertise and field service—so the company abandoned trying to handle everything and instead shifted to selling only core components.
item.content:encoded:
In full-body infrared medical screening, Gaode Zhigan's (高德质感) technology provides only 10% of the diagnostic service's value, with the other 90% coming from medical expertise and field service—so the company abandoned trying to handle everything and instead shifted to selling only core components.

How a subsidiary of a traditional hard-tech public company spent a decade iterating through civilian use cases with clear decision logic and concrete details—for anyone concerned with commercializing technology.

4:16 Every object emits light you cannot see
The physics of infrared is that any object with temperature emits infrared light due to molecular thermal motion; the longer the wavelength diverges from the visible spectrum, the higher its correlation with temperature. What a detector does is capture the extremely faint infrared signal from an object miles away, causing a temperature change of just fractions of a degree on the detector's surface and reading it out. It must both maintain temperature to preserve the faint signal and dissipate heat quickly to enable continuous imaging—this is the technically hardest part.

6:52 Finding a lost cat was a use case the makers didn't anticipate
Infrared equipment was initially positioned for hunting and finding wildlife, but customers reported that when domestic cats go missing and hide in grass, they can't be found by calling or by eye. A sweep with infrared reveals a bright dot—get there and it's the cat. This civilian use case was not designed by the company; users discovered it themselves and fed back the insight.

14:25 Infrared catches power grid failures before equipment breaks
Electrical anomalies like poor contact or short circuits first produce localized temperature spikes, and infrared inspection discovers aging components before equipment truly breaks down, causing breaker trips and blackouts—allowing engineers to plan replacement of backup equipment and avoid large-scale outages. Huang Sheng (黄胜) noted that the 1970s-80s generation experienced frequent childhood power outages, whereas now there are fewer, which relates to infrared technology's widespread adoption in power systems.

27:44 When you provide 10% of the value, you shouldn't fight for the other 90%
In scenarios like full-body infrared medical screening, infrared is just one critical technical point in the diagnostic process; medical expertise, theoretical backing, and field service constitute ninety percent of the entire diagnostic and customer service chain. The company concluded that rather than filling gaps in capabilities it doesn't understand, it's better to do only what it does best—that ten percent—and sell equipment or chip modules to partners who truly understand medicine and Chinese medicine theory, letting them handle the remaining ninety percent. This decision determines which tracks the company runs end-to-end products (like airport body-temperature screening, where the process is simple and requires no diagnostic judgment) and which it supplies components for.

32:45 Competitors losing money does not mean the market doesn't exist
When the company evaluated potential businesses, it didn't just look at whether it would make or lose money; it also analyzed why competitors lose money—is it because the market itself has no demand, or because others haven't found the right approach? Judging whether you have an advantage to turn a money-losing business into a profitable one is the key step in deciding whether to enter a new scenario, rather than simply abandoning the entire direction because others are losing money.

34:18 Once spun off, nobody sets problems for them to solve anymore
After Gaode Zhigan (高德质感) spun off from Gaode Hongwai (高德红外) as an independent civilian company, the organization initially retained the habit of passively receiving requirements—business units would ask power grids what they needed and directly make that the product direction. But it turned out that different provincial power grids had very different needs, making it impossible to produce a single form factor satisfying all customers, with R&D costs too high. The company therefore established a dedicated product department and marketing department to synthesize scattered front-line requirements into a single product proposal acceptable to most customers, then hand it to R&D—essentially the organization had to learn to set its own problems.

37:23 AI improves how images look, but doesn't command higher prices
AI applications at Gaode Zhigan fall into two categories: one is imperceptible to users, such as using machine learning to optimize image brightness adjustment in high-light and low-light scenarios, making pictures look more comfortable—but this upgrade won't make the product sell for more; it's only a user-experience improvement. The other category is recognizing the photographed object (such as transformers or insulators) and providing more appropriate algorithms and shooting recommendations, helping power-grid engineers complete inspections more efficiently—an auxiliary function rather than an independent selling point.

42:18 Data centers consume electricity, which means infrared has business opportunities
Infrared directly relates to energy flows: major producers like petroleum, natural gas, solar, and wind power, as well as major consumers like metallurgy, all need infrared for monitoring and maintenance. Huang Sheng (黄胜) believes that as AI compute centers become a new major energy consumer and scale up, they will also pull the infrared industry along—though not as directly as how the optical-module industry was directly boosted by AI.

item.title: Partnership law firms can collapse even with zero debt and rising profits
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-oddlots-合伙制律所能在零负债-利润仍增长时突然倒闭/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-oddlots-合伙制律所能在零负债-利润仍增长时突然倒闭/
item.description: A 95-year-old Wall Street law firm with no major debt and rising profits collapsed within months like a bank run because its growth lagged competitors, proving partnerships fail from relative underperformance, not absolute financial decline.
item.content:encoded:
A 95-year-old Wall Street law firm with no major debt and rising profits collapsed within months like a bank run because its growth lagged competitors, proving partnerships fail from relative underperformance, not absolute financial decline.

The guest's academic papers predicted this collapse nearly point-by-point, concentrated on equity structure and bankruptcy mechanics rather than law firm gossip, densely argued and worth hearing in full.

5:04 Partnership law firms persist for historical and regulatory reasons, not efficiency
Partnership structures everywhere require partner ownership for three reasons. First, historically, starting a law practice required only labor, not capital. Second, state bar ethics rules mandate that lawyers own their firms. But the deeper explanation comes from Yale economist Henry Hansman: lawyers' output (billable hours traced to specific clients) is measurable in ways factory workers' output isn't, so partnerships create fewer internal profit-allocation disputes than worker ownership models. This measurability advantage is why Hansman's theory predicts partnerships over employee ownership schemes like at General Motors.

12:14 A key partner's departure triggers the run because costs don't fall with revenue
When a star partner leaves, clients follow almost immediately—revenue vanishes overnight. But office leases, pension obligations, and the salaries of junior partners who depended on that partner's client base don't shrink. If that partner was generating more revenue than his own compensation, his departure is pure loss. The profit pool that remaining partners split shrinks directly, forcing compensation cuts—and that's where the run begins.

14:17 Partner distributions become clawable at bankruptcy once the firm goes insolvent
Partners don't receive wages; they receive discretionary profit distributions, legally equivalent to dividends. Once a firm is declared insolvent, any further distributions to partners can be clawed back by creditors under fraudulent transfer law. This creates a calculation every partner silently runs: money in my pocket now might have to go back later.

18:23 Each partner constantly weighs leaving by expected value of compensation
Take a partner at Weil in September expecting $2 million in January. But if the firm has a 50% chance of collapsing by February, that $2 million is really worth only $1 million in expectation. If Gibson Dunn offers $1.5 million with lower failure risk, that's actually higher expected value—appearing to be a pay cut while genuinely being a raise. Every partner is quietly solving this problem. Once enough partners get the same answer, the run begins.

21:25 Falling in the rankings is more fatal than falling profits
Economist Morley's papers predicted exactly this scenario: a firm could collapse despite zero major debt and continued profit growth, provided growth lagged competitors. Weil's per-partner profit ranking fell from #9 in 2020 to #20 in 2025, while profits kept rising every year—just not as fast as Kirkland's. Weil got stuck: too small to be a megaplatform, too big to be a boutique like Wachtell or Cravath.

28:31 Partners' equity vanishes at retirement, so nobody invests for the future
A Microsoft shareholder can hold forever; future value gets priced into trading. A law firm partner's equity expires at retirement—no buyback, no perpetuity. This creates generational conflict: a 31-year-old partner might invest in the firm's future; a 61-year-old retiring in two years has zero incentive. This explains why law firms won't spend heavily to build AI systems that pay off in five years—because today's decision-makers won't be there to enjoy the returns.

36:42 Investor-owned law firms survive runs because partners aren't owners
Australian law firm Slater & Gordon is listed and investor-owned. Its Quindel acquisition turned out to be fraud, leaving the company insolvent. But because lawyers don't own the firm, management could wipe out shareholder equity and hand creditors the company as new shareholders in a restructuring—while lawyers kept their salaries and jobs, like Delta Airlines pilots. At a partnership like Weil, if you tried the same move, every partner walks to Cravath the next morning.

47:54 Law firms will lease AI like office space, not build it
Generational conflict means today's partners won't fund AI that pays off in five years, since different partners will be there then. Firms will license and rent AI technology like they lease offices—not own it like they'd buy a building. Kirkland & Ellis' $500 million AI program over five years looks ambitious until you note their ~$10 billion annual revenue—it's a rounding error, and they've paced it to sync with revenue growth, not to get ahead of it.

item.title: One pot of wheat and the refusal to experiment: how the Soviet agronomist starved his peers and the nation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-cautionary-苏联农学家靠一盆花拒绝做实验-饿死了同行也没喂饱苏联/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-cautionary-苏联农学家靠一盆花拒绝做实验-饿死了同行也没喂饱苏联/
item.description: Lysenko said "hunger does not wait" and refused field trials, declaring success from a single wheat plant in a flowerpot; Borlaug faced the same famine but fed Mexico with more rigorous control experiments.
item.content:encoded:
Lysenko said "hunger does not wait" and refused field trials, declaring success from a single wheat plant in a flowerpot; Borlaug faced the same famine but fed Mexico with more rigorous control experiments.

An excellent pair of contrasts: facing the same pressure of "no time for experiments," one abandoned scientific method toward disaster, the other upheld it to create the Green Revolution—worth hearing in full.

10:07 Two and a half years to breed new wheat—with only a flowerpot
Stalin demanded agricultural experts compress the breeding cycle from ten to twelve years to four or five. Scientists said it was impossible. Lysenko claimed he had done it in two and a half years. His method: skip the laborious field trials and arrange a few flowerpots in a greenhouse corner, relying on his invented "plant development stage theory" to predict crossing results. His justification: people were starving, and scientists had no right to waste a year on field trials.

12:11 From 500 surveys, published 50—and claimed victory anyway
Lysenko asked 500 farms to test his summer potato method and submit reports. Because they knew he was Stalin's favorite, the responses were likely biased favorably. He published only 50 of them anyway, claiming the results "completely proved the possibility of doubled yields." The show notes the logical error: try any new method across 500 random locations and some will succeed by coincidence. You cannot ignore the many failures. But Lysenko reasoned otherwise: farms that failed must have been lazy, incompetent, or deliberately sabotaging.

14:20 Vavilov begged Stalin face-to-face and heard he was just "tinkering with plants"
Vavilov was an internationally renowned geneticist who tried to persuade the authorities to stop ideological attacks on scientists. He even obtained a solo meeting with Stalin.
