Face-to-face, Stalin told him he only "tinkered with plants" and spouted "botanical nonsense," unlike Lysenko who truly helped agriculture. Vavilov understood he was in danger. In 1940, during a wheat field inspection, secret police arrested him. A month later he was forced to "confess" to being a "saboteur," sentenced to twenty years hard labor, and died in prison from hunger.

18:34 Borlaug broke the textbook rules for site selection—and moved to a rat-infested ruin
The Rockefeller Foundation's agricultural textbook required new varieties to be developed near where farmers actually planted. Borlaug wanted to establish a second base in northwest Mexico with a different climate—he could grow two crops a year there, accelerating trials. His supervisor refused at first because the Foundation had no work permits in that region. Borlaug insisted on taking the risk anyway. He took over an abandoned research station alone: fields overgrown with weeds, windows broken, no sanitation, rats running at night. He swept dead rats off the floor to make his bed, built fires from corn cobs to cook canned beans, and rebuilt the station from scratch.

20:39 Rabbits could become chickens: Lysenko declared all of genetics bourgeois pseudoscience
Lysenko did not stop at agriculture. He declared the entire field of genetics to be a bourgeois doctrine, mocking Mendel and Morgan's theory of "hereditary particles" as nonsense. He believed acquired characteristics could directly pass to the next generation, and claimed he could transform wheat into rye, hornbeam into hazel, even rabbits into chickens by adjusting conditions. At a 1948 conference, he produced a report personally approved by Stalin. After that, Soviet biology textbooks were rewritten, research institutes dissolved, researchers fired, and genetics research was completely banned in the USSR.

32:08 The bird-chasing boy whose pollination method saved Borlaug years of labor
Borlaug hired local boys including Reyes Vega to chase birds away from wheat. One boy asked if they could try extracting pollen sacs from wheat spikes using tweezers for hand pollination. Borlaug agreed. Reyes quickly became more skilled than Borlaug himself and invented a new method: one cut to open the spike and extract all pollen sacs at once. Borlaug later said this uneducated boy's discovery saved them years of labor.

34:16 Lysenko could not set up a control plot—yet he was Soviet biology's highest authority
After Stalin died, a visitor toured Lysenko's experimental fields. He saw a plot with the new fertilizer formula growing well and asked to see a control plot with the same seed but different fertilizer. Lysenko said there was none. The visitor then found another plot labeled "new formula applied" growing poorly. Lysenko explained that the fertilizer worker must have made a mistake. The episode's point: as the USSR's highest biological authority, Lysenko never grasped the most basic principle of scientific method—the control group.

40:38 Lysenko never repented, yet he identified a real problem in science
In 1971, an American writer dined with elderly Lysenko. Lysenko remained angry and indignant, insisting his knowledge came from field work while Vavilov's people relied on books and laboratories. The show concedes Lysenko's diagnosis of the "problem" was not entirely wrong: academic researchers do sometimes work too comfortably in ivory towers, disconnected from real problems they should solve, and intelligent young people without formal education can discover things scholars miss. But the crucial difference: facing the same problem, Borlaug chose to use better scientific tools, while Lysenko chose to abandon scientific tools altogether.

item.title: Huang's Ouster Isn't Scandal but Washington's Long-Overdue Reckoning with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-sharptech-黄仁勋下台不是桃色事件-是华盛顿对英伟达积怨已久的总清算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-sharptech-黄仁勋下台不是桃色事件-是华盛顿对英伟达积怨已久的总清算/
item.description: Nvidia's repeated defiance of China export policy and the national security system was the true trigger for Huang's forced exit; the sex scandal was merely the final straw.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's repeated defiance of China export policy and the national security system was the true trigger for Huang's forced exit; the sex scandal was merely the final straw.

The first half systematically traces Nvidia's origins and governance structure; the middle section's debate over chip export-control logic is the most valuable part of the episode—listen through to get the full picture.

4:11 An affair with subordinates is ironclad grounds for board removal
The hosts first clarify an often-overlooked governance issue: boards are supposed to represent shareholders, but they also have motives that don't align with shareholder interests—like protecting their own seats. But this time is different. In US corporate culture, romantic relationships with subordinates cross a clear, irrefutable red line. Once established, a board has almost no choice but to fire, even if the stock price drops double digits, even if employees and most shareholders would prefer otherwise.

16:31 Nvidia doesn't sell chips, it sells systems
Around 2019, Huang's crucial move was acquiring Mellanox: he recognized not faster individual chips, but the system capability of linking multiple chips via high-speed interconnect into a single logical system, later evolving into MVLink. Nvidia's moat isn't just CUDA but this: selling systems, not chips. AMD's previous-generation chips had better single-chip performance, but AMD doesn't build systems—that game AMD simply never entered.

20:35 Huang went all-out to keep Nvidia from becoming another Intel
If buyers were only Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic—a handful of megacustomers—they'd have the negotiating power to crush Nvidia's margins, exactly what happened to Intel when negotiating with AMD. Huang aggressively backed Neoclouds and various new labs, deliberately creating more buyers to avoid becoming a small number of giants' captive supplier. This wasn't charity.

1:03:01 Downgraded-spec chips destroyed Nvidia's relationship with national security officials
Biden's first version of China chip sanctions limited memory bandwidth, not compute. Within a month, Huang released lower-bandwidth, worse-performing ‘compliant’ chips and continued selling heavily into China. Technically legal, but the security establishment saw this as open defiance. From that day on, the national security system branded Nvidia a ‘bad actor’ and Huang branded them ‘idiots.’ Their relationship became adversarial—this was the beginning of what became the final reckoning.

1:09:01 Export bans have made Chinese chip independence a necessity
The core argument against chip bans: you can't conjure a chip ecosystem just by throwing money at it—Microsoft spent billions and couldn't save Windows Phone. As long as Nvidia chips are available, no Chinese government mandate can force programmers to abandon CUDA for alternatives. But a complete cutoff creates a hard necessity for independence—undoing fifty years of US tech-transfer management strategy.

1:17:05 Corruption allegations changed the character of the entire affair
Beyond chip exports and policy shifts, a third layer of anger stems from more direct corruption suspicions—like the Trump family's financial interests in Malaysian data centers. The hosts argue that even if you can understand the Trump team's positions on China policy, adding corruption poisons the entire affair. Huang's scandal became a single outlet for all the accumulated resentment.

1:18:05 Nvidia's supplier financing model faces its biggest test
Nvidia has played banker to its ecosystem, rolling free cash flow into debt into equity investments, essentially bridging the entire AI bubble. Whether the interim CEO and CFO will continue Huang's aggressive supplier financing is an open question—and credit tightening in the Neocloud market actually began three months before the scandal, making the stock drop less damaging than what's coming.

item.title: Physical AI founder bets hardware first: when foundation models arrive, pure models thin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-latetalk-物理ai创始人提前押注硬件-基模一来-模型就会变薄/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-latetalk-物理ai创始人提前押注硬件-基模一来-模型就会变薄/
item.description: When Liu Songming founded LiberAI, he predicted foundation models like GPT-6 Astra would consume System 2—the perception and planning layer of embodied AI. From day one, he chose hardware and product as the moat instead of building a pure model company.
item.content:encoded:
When Liu Songming founded LiberAI, he predicted foundation models like GPT-6 Astra would consume System 2—the perception and planning layer of embodied AI. From day one, he chose hardware and product as the moat instead of building a pure model company.

Information density concentrates in the second half: how glove data approximates or surpasses teleoperation at lower cost, and why hardware-model coupling runs deeper than the founder expected. The first 25 minutes on growth history can be skipped.

25:17 Technical judgment, not industry connections, drives early-stage capital decisions
Industry convention pairs young technical talent with a veteran industry executive. Liu chose differently. At this stage, the company's biggest expenditure is compute and data collection. Deciding where that money goes and which technical paths to pursue requires technical judgment, not just resource coordination. Without it, capital efficiency collapses.

35:23 Foundation models will consume the perception layer, squeezing pure robotics companies
Liu maps robot-world interaction into three layers: System 2 (perception, planning, reasoning), System 1 (converting instructions to action sequences), System 0 (low-level motor control). Through 2023-24, venture capital believed embodied companies could own all three layers and scale toward AGI. Liu predicted from day one that foundation models would inevitably capture System 2. GPT-6 Astra's arrival proved it. This makes pure-model robotics startups dangerously thin. LiberAI chose full-stack from inception—using hardware and product to thicken the narrowing moat.

59:37 Glove data with 25% teleoperation outperforms 100% teleoperation alone
Experiments show glove data combined with 25% real-robot teleoperation data outperforms models trained on 100% real-robot teleoperation alone. Teleoperation isn't perfect: operators watch sideways while robots move forward, creating a viewpoint mismatch with the robot's camera. Lack of force feedback makes operators slow. This motion pattern diverges from smooth human actions in internet videos. Gloves worn on human hands align naturally with human motion and extract knowledge from internet videos more effectively.

1:19:43 Hardware constraints go deeper into performance than training recipes can fix
The biggest surprise wasn't training—it was hardware. Different morphologies and sensor choices affect final performance far more than expected, and this impact can't be recovered through later training approaches. System 0 motor control algorithms couple deeply with System 1 action generation. Motor control couples tightly with the robot's joint structure, DOF, and motor parameters. This demonstrates hardware companies' structural advantage over pure model companies—but it also means iteration speed is constrained by hardware's long development cycles.

1:36:56 Foundation model labs lack the character for robotics' unglamorous delivery work
Consider rumors of OpenAI or Anthropic acquiring Physical Intelligence, and potential entry by carmakers or Huawei. Liu argues that real competition only emerges at delivery scale, where every customer is a hardened negotiation. This work demands patience that OpenAI likely lacks, and the incentives don't align: the same engineering effort applied to software yields 20x growth. Why chase service and manufacturing margins? Liu judges the real threat is non-standard automation specialists and prior-generation delivery firms.

1:48:01 Physical robotics will eventually consolidate into an Apple-scale giant
Liu expects physical AI applications to transition from today's fragmented commercial and industrial niches toward consolidation. Eventually a mega-company emerges at Apple's scale—among the greatest industrial products in human history. This company likely emerges from firms already pursuing full-stack, hardware-first approaches. This is what LiberAI positions as its highest-probability wager.

2:00:06 Build organizations that question decisions made too fast with too little information
Liu reflects on past errors: mistakes often stem not from bad option selection but from deciding too fast on incomplete information. People unconsciously filter incoming data through existing expectations. This trap is especially dangerous in familiar domains, where strong priors tempt you to skip verification. The remedy: deliberately preserve diverse voices and cultivate people who can stand up and audit—to coordinate information gaps and misaligned goals—rather than relying on one founder's final call.

item.title: Liangpei wants users to leave fast—that's exactly how it makes money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-wangqinwen-良配巴不得用户尽快离开-这恰恰是它的赚钱逻辑/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-wangqinwen-良配巴不得用户尽快离开-这恰恰是它的赚钱逻辑/
item.description: Liangpei (良配) sells memberships that can't be renewed; users leave once they match. The faster they go, the fewer tokens the platform burns—exactly opposite to most AI products profiting from retention.
item.content:encoded:
Liangpei (良配) sells memberships that can't be renewed; users leave once they match. The faster they go, the fewer tokens the platform burns—exactly opposite to most AI products profiting from retention.

A story of a former Kimi employee who spent 8 years accumulating resources and raised 15 million in 3 hours; the middle section clarifies traditional matchmaker schemes, and the second half breaks down AI dating business models in detail, with information density concentrated in the middle and later sections.

3:00 Traditional matchmakers price by what you can pay, not what service costs
Zeng Xinxun notes that among 150 couples who registered at Shenzhen's Civil Affairs Bureau, fewer than 5 percent succeeded through professional matchmakers. Traditional matchmakers don't price based on the service itself, but first probe your willingness to pay and credit card limits—the same service sells for 20,000, 30,000 or 50,000 yuan depending on how much you can afford. More egregiously, some agencies pressure young women to take loans, using the pitch ‘it's better to find a husband than buy a handbag’ to package dating as an investment.

21:15 Grassroots teams lack resources to compete with well-funded rivals
Zeng ran a campus food delivery platform in university that generated over 10 million yuan in annual revenue at peak, but was completely shut out when Ele.me raised 80 million dollars and rapidly expanded to 200 cities. He concluded this wasn't a product or execution problem, but that grassroots teams lack the resources to race against opponents already backed by capital markets—which is why he spent 8 years before this venture deliberately ‘accumulating equipment’ (technology, team, industry credentials).

37:23 Three hours to raise 15 million required eight years of prep
A week after resigning as CTO of Kimi, Zeng met with investors; by chance at a hackathon café, he talked for 15 minutes with someone from Jujin Capital, who immediately called to verify his Kimi background and set up a meeting with Xu Xin the next day. In three hours of negotiation, Xu Xin proactively offered to provide the full 15 million yuan representing 20 percent equity in one payment, with zero protective clauses in the agreement. Zeng says this wasn't luck, but the accumulated technology, team, and industry credentials he'd built over 8 years all materializing at that moment.

44:29 Four structural flaws prevent dating apps from helping you pair up
Zeng identifies four categories of problems in existing dating products: platforms mix users with different needs to boost DAU, with profiles limited to 100-150 characters creating severe information shortage; an endless stream of candidates creates the illusion of abundance, making people constantly compare and undervalue the person in front of them; and the platform's business model rewards longer user stays, giving it no incentive to actually help you find someone, putting user and platform interests fundamentally at odds.

47:31 Single-match design escapes the user-platform prisoner's dilemma
Liangpei designed the EV1 matching mechanism, which doesn't offer a continuous candidate pool but shows one person at a time. Zeng believes previous products didn't dare try this because match success rates were too low—EV1's risk directly exposes you to the 1-minus-success-rate failure probability; Liangpei only dared build EV1 because AI collected two to three thousand characters of context, raising match accuracy high enough to support it.

50:36 Only non-renewable memberships make platforms want you to succeed
Liangpei's core memberships are non-renewable: the 2,000 yuan ‘guaranteed marriage membership’ keeps the payment if users marry within three years, otherwise fully refunded; there's also a 1,000 yuan perpetual membership paid in one lump sum. Zeng explains the design works because the platform burns tokens daily for each user, and the longer users stay the higher the cost, so the platform naturally wants users matched quickly and gone—the opposite of most software that profits from renewal and time spent.

53:37 Acquisition cost rose from a few yuan to over 50
In 2018-19 doing campus delivery, acquiring a user cost just a few yuan, but today in the two-sided market Liangpei faces, 50 yuan acquisition cost isn't enough. In the first week after launch, Zeng watched growth curves daily with anxiety, because the earliest users trusted the product most but experienced the smallest sample size and matching pool, until a few articles went viral and user scale picked up.

56:39 Betting everything on one path beats hedging between many options
Zeng says at every major inflection point in his life he chose only one path—applied to only Southern University of Science and Technology for college, picked one place when job hunting and went there, and for this venture only does dating, something he experienced personally, rather than the billion-dollar-market spaces investors suggested. He believes that with multiple choices you fall into decision paralysis, efficiency drops lowest, and going all-in actually provides clarity.

item.title: Riding a trend is 1% of success; being the right person is 99%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhangxiaojun-踩中风口在成功里只占1-99-是你是不是那块料/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhangxiaojun-踩中风口在成功里只占1-99-是你是不是那块料/
item.description: Liang Qiwei draws on years of game-making to argue: trends and capital narratives can sustain short-term revenue, but what truly determines fate is the creator's character, not external circumstances.
item.content:encoded:
Liang Qiwei draws on years of game-making to argue: trends and capital narratives can sustain short-term revenue, but what truly determines fate is the creator's character, not external circumstances.

Most of the conversation explores wuxia aesthetics and literary theory; the truly valuable startup retrospective and self-examination come in the second half—listen past the midpoint.

1:05 The core of the knight-errant is not goodness, but willingness to risk greatly
Liang Qiwei rejects equating the knight-errant with the everyday good person (like helping an elderly woman cross the street). True knights-errant must, driven by hatred and injustice, choose to bear risk with superhuman resolve—if you're not exposed to real danger, you're just a good person. This also explains why knights-errant are always outsiders: the rivers and lakes stand against the state; knights have no power to enforce law, only to maintain justice where order collapses.

33:31 Players see through any moral label you attach
When the team tried to add direct dialogue like "For nation and people, that is the great knight-errant" to give the game moral weight, players almost universally rejected it. The problem wasn't disagreement with the sentiment itself, Liang explains, but that players saw through the creative intent: you're not thinking about the game itself, you're trying to borrow external moral associations for mainstream approval. The lesson became: convey the spirit obliquely, never through self-congratulatory statements.

1:12:10 In school he was the invisible man in the dorm
Liang Qiwei recalls having Asperger's-like traits—indifferent to the real world, acutely sensitive to the virtual. In his dorm, he wasn't bullied; he was "transparent." Roommates gradually stopped inviting him to meals, and he felt no loneliness, because loneliness presumes a desire for companionship he simply didn't experience. The term itself mischaracterized his state.

1:52:48 One failed exam erased his entire life plan
Liang was on track: fifth in his class, accepted to Tsinghua for graduate study through the direct enrollment track. Then he failed engineering economics, an unprecedented system failure—the rules said you could advance to Tsinghua but couldn't graduate. Like learning there is no final boss before the climax, the world suddenly unraveled. But it was also the first time fate loosened its grip on his predetermined path as a "problem-solver."

2:34:31 During the capital boom, the team forgot how to do real work
After Blade of Shadow I found early success—twenty people, a couple million yuan monthly profit—the company dreamed bigger: anime, series, IP matrices, even pitching for a New Third Board listing. For years, Liang's actual work was pitching to investors, cutting deals at dinners, spinning IP narratives. Real coding and art happened less than a day per week. He compares it to martial artists who haven't drawn a real blade in years; when actual combat comes, they're finished in one stroke.

2:44:38 Professing purity is the start of impurity
Liang reflects on an article he wrote years ago: humble-bragging about colleagues' raises and a new girlfriend abroad. He sees it now as commodifying pure creative experience into capital-market small talk—using claims of "purity" to prove he'd learned the money game. Two selves were fighting: one faithful to first principles, one increasingly shrewd, hunting for external validation.

3:01:53 Chasing trends is 1% of success; capability is 99%
Blade of Shadow II deliberately stacked two trends: mobile esports and anime culture. It succeeded at neither. Liang's conclusion: catching a trend accounts for maybe 1% of success; 99% depends on internal capability—whether the team actually has what it takes to execute the vision. External conditions are irrelevant if you're not the person built for this work. No market opens for those not suited to seize it.

3:23:06 Brilliant Murong Fu always loses to clumsy Guo Jing
Game Science and miHoYo succeeded through what Liang calls "strong-mind thinking": the conviction that markets aren't fixed, that force of will can reshape them. Liang admits to the opposite—the "problem-solver" mentality: solve what's given, never imagine changing the game itself. In wuxia metaphor, Murong Fu—brilliant, elaborate, overthinking—always falls to apparently simple Guo Jing. True strength is internal, inward-facing, not in displayed talent.

item.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO over espionage scandal; company has no successor internally
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-hardfork-黄仁勋因间谍绯闻辞任英伟达ceo-公司内部找不到能接替他的人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-hardfork-黄仁勋因间谍绯闻辞任英伟达ceo-公司内部找不到能接替他的人/
item.description: The incoming CFO can only be an interim CEO, because Nvidia's helmsman must be both a top computer scientist and a strong enough executive to browbeat Taiwan suppliers—a combination only Jensen Huang possesses today.
item.content:encoded:
The incoming CFO can only be an interim CEO, because Nvidia's helmsman must be both a top computer scientist and a strong enough executive to browbeat Taiwan suppliers—a combination only Jensen Huang possesses today.

One episode gives you the complete chain of events, the board's motives, and the succession puzzle—high information density, though the ending's jokes about memes can be skipped.

1:00 Resignation wasn't one scandal—it was scandal stacked upon scandal
The trigger for Huang's resignation wasn't a single scandal but escalation in layers: first the revelation of a relationship with Alice Wong (suspected Chinese spy), then a separate exposure of a long-running affair with Kimberly Powell, the medical-division VP reporting directly to him. The board convened overnight and announced his resignation before market open. The show frames this as a twist in a spy story—two relationships stacked together finally broke his position.

6:19 The board wanted to keep him, but finances changed the math
Multiple board members hold over $1 billion in Nvidia stock each. Huang has been the only CEO in the company's 33-year history, so by normal logic they would have moved to protect him. But the scandal had already tanked the stock price, and keeping him would only expand the losses. Stephen Witt argues the board's decision was a financial calculation to protect shareholder value, not a moral judgment.

8:31 The commerce secretary ran interference for Huang inside government
Commerce Secretary Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Bessent clashed directly over whether to add Megaspeed to the trade blacklist and whether to close regulatory loopholes in Southeast Asia data centers. Lutnick had been seen as the force inside government delaying export controls to protect Huang's interests. With Huang's fall, Congressional and internal-government pressure to tighten China-related chip restrictions has visibly intensified.

17:02 He saw the world as he wished it to be
Anna Swanson argues Huang consistently denied the existence of chip-smuggling problems for years, even as US authorities uncovered large-scale smuggling cases. Her assessment: this trait—seeing the world as one wishes it to be—was both the source of his long success and possibly the root of his collapse.

26:24 Finding a successor is like replacing Michael Jordan
Stephen Witt frames the succession problem this way: it's like asking ‘who replaces Michael Jordan after he leaves the Bulls?’—there's no ready replacement. Huang had to be a top computer scientist, a fierce enough executive to browbeat Taiwan suppliers, someone able to schmooze clients and call Trump directly. These skills rarely appear in one person; the company essentially needs three people to fill his void.

28:35 The CFO doesn't understand transistors; she can only be temporary
Interim CEO Colette Kress is widely seen as a transitional choice: she's an excellent financial executive but not a world-class computer scientist, and a chip company's CEO must truly understand the technical details from transistors to data centers. Inside Nvidia, talents like Ian Buck excel at engineering but lack experience with customers and suppliers. Finding someone with both sets of skills is extremely difficult.

31:53 Financial disclosures shifted quietly as the scandal simmered
As the scandal festered last year, Nvidia abruptly changed how it disclosed revenue—making it harder to track what percentage of revenue came from Singapore and Malaysia. Anna Swanson points out this is precisely when the Southeast Asian business surge into China (that journalists were trying to document) got deliberately obscured. Colette Kress, as CFO, would have been deeply involved in such financial-disclosure decisions.

38:06 Thirty days ago he wielded enormous power; today he has none
Stephen Witt describes the collapse as Greek tragedy: thirty days ago Huang was one of the most powerful people in AI; now he holds 3% of Nvidia—still valuable—but has no executive power and Trump won't take his calls anymore. The show suggests this illustrates a deeper truth: even in the age of AI, the endings are written by human weakness, not technology itself.

item.title: Suharto burned Borneo's peatlands into disaster trying to salvage his political legacy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-asianometry-苏哈托为挽救政治声誉-把婆罗洲泥炭地烧成了灾难/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-asianometry-苏哈托为挽救政治声誉-把婆罗洲泥炭地烧成了灾难/
item.description: Suharto pushed a million-hectare rice project to sustain his 'Father of Development' reputation, but peatlands proved unsuitable for farming and planning failures triggered what became one of Southeast Asia's largest single-year carbon-release fire events.
item.content:encoded:
Suharto pushed a million-hectare rice project to sustain his 'Father of Development' reputation, but peatlands proved unsuitable for farming and planning failures triggered what became one of Southeast Asia's largest single-year carbon-release fire events.

A real case of political obsession overriding scientific judgment, with staggering numbers and straightforward narrative—easy to follow in one commute.

4:12 Rice shortages destabilized Sukarno and enabled Suharto to seize power
Under Sukarno, rice was more than food—it was hard currency for military and bureaucratic salaries and was prioritized for foreign exchange. Sukarno's rice quotas mobilized the country but backfired: rice did not reach deficit regions, foreign exchange went to imported rice instead of needed fertilizer, Javanese paddies degraded, and output fell 13.6% between 1960 and 1964. The crisis destabilized his regime and handed Suharto the opening for his coup.

6:18 Oil windfall from 1973 embargo made Indonesia's rice self-sufficiency possible
Suharto took power just as the Green Revolution introduced high-yield varieties IR8 and IR5, and Indonesia caught the 1973 Middle East oil embargo windfall: annual petroleum revenue spiked above $5 billion. This money subsidized fertilizer permanently, set a rice price floor, and built irrigation canals and roads. Rice output soared from 12 million tons in 1969 to 22 million tons by 1981. By 1984, Indonesia declared rice self-sufficiency—the foundation of Suharto's "Father of Development" reputation.

7:22 Rice production stalled in the 1990s while population kept growing
By the 1990s, rice output growth collapsed to 0.5–1% annually while population grew 1–2% yearly. Late-1980s urban development claimed about 20% of Java's best farmland. Severe floods and droughts compounded the problem. By 1992, Indonesia returned to rice imports for the first time in a decade; the 1995 drought forced imports of 3 million tons. The loss threatened Suharto's political foundation.

13:38 Peatlands unsuitable for rice farming was established science by the 1970s
The Dayak indigenous people had for generations grown rice only on coastal, shallower, relatively fertile peatlands, and even there harvests were often poor due to unpredictable rainfall. Indonesia's Bogor Soil Research Institute had classified such interior peatlands as "problem soils" since 1974. Yet after visiting a successful Singaporean-Chinese operation on Sumatra's coast, Suharto decided to replicate the model on the completely different deep inland peatlands of Central Kalimantan, ignoring the geological difference and existing scientific conclusions.

16:40 Suharto demanded results by 1997 so construction began before studies finished
Suharto demanded the first harvest by 1997, so construction started in January 1996 before cost-benefit analysis, engineering studies, or environmental impact assessments were complete. Most Indonesian companies and international investors refused to participate; a longtime Suharto contractor reportedly joined only to avoid losing other government contracts. Environmental group WALI tried exposing the threat to endangered orangutans and ecosystems, but could not stop the project.

17:41 Massive drainage canals destroyed peatlands while resettlement housing barely got built
Thousands of kilometers of drainage canals were poorly planned—they cut directly across major peatland domes and systematically drained the layers of water. The plan called for 20,000 homes for Javanese settlers within two years; after ten months, only 600 were built. For Suharto's April 1997 inspection, authorities built a helicopter pad and temporarily replanted rice seedlings to show prosperity. He stayed two hours, announced the project a success, and left.

18:41 Half a million hectares burned in 1997, sending smoke across Southeast Asia
Forest cleared, peatlands dried, illegal burning for clearance sparked fires that satellites detected as early as January 1997. In 1997 alone, over 500,000 hectares of the 1.4 million-hectare zone burned, 80% of it peatland. The carbon released from peat averaging 51 centimeters thick was enormous. Fires flared repeatedly until the June 1998 rains; the total burned area reached roughly 10 million hectares, smoke drifted to Singapore and Malaysia, and the region's carbon emissions were among the largest single-year increases on record.

21:51 Billions spent but left Dayak people and settlers both empty-handed
The project was budgeted at $2–3 billion, partly from Indonesia's "Reforestation Fund." Much money vanished into corruption and fake subcontracts. The Dayak were promised investment and prosperity; instead their farmland burned, fishponds were destroyed by canals, and traditional territory fell to settlers. Some 15,000 Javanese families who relocated found almost no infrastructure. After Suharto fell in 1998 amid the Asian financial crisis, the new government formally canceled the project in 1999.

item.title: Shelved forty years, an old Alzheimer's theory finds vindication in imaging
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-sciencepod-阿尔茨海默病老牌假说被雪藏四十年-影像证据证明它可能是对的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-sciencepod-阿尔茨海默病老牌假说被雪藏四十年-影像证据证明它可能是对的/
item.description: A young scientist uses imaging data to show that degradation of deep-brain cholinergic neurons precedes, rather than follows, cortical amyloid deposition—reviving an old theory sidelined by the amyloid hypothesis.
item.content:encoded:
A young scientist uses imaging data to show that degradation of deep-brain cholinergic neurons precedes, rather than follows, cortical amyloid deposition—reviving an old theory sidelined by the amyloid hypothesis.

Three interviews, each densely packed: why a neuroscience theory is making a comeback, why America's electricity crisis is institutional rather than technical, and how a massive genetic dataset reshapes prescribing.

2:04 Drug-induced amnesia led researchers to the cholinergic hypothesis
Researchers discovered that drugs blocking acetylcholine signaling induced a memory deficit resembling that seen in aging and early Alzheimer's. Subsequent autopsy studies found that the nucleus basalis of Meynert—a deep-brain hub where cholinergic neurons project to cortical memory and attention areas—was severely damaged late in disease. This led pathologists to suspect it was among the earliest damaged structures. By the early 1980s these findings coalesced into the cholinergic hypothesis: Alzheimer's memory loss and age-related memory loss might be the same process, differing only in degree.

8:14 The amyloid hypothesis displaced both the old theory and old drugs
When the amyloid hypothesis was formally proposed in the early 1990s, a cohort of cholinergic molecules already showing promise—including drugs targeting cognitive receptors with fewer side effects—was shelved outright. The entire field pivoted to focus on the protein deemed the culprit. Mutations in familial Alzheimer's patients all pointed to amyloid generation pathways; the evidence seemed "locked in," and cholinergic research was crowded out of mainstream view.

9:20 Amyloid drugs clear plaques beautifully but barely improve cognition
Anti-amyloid antibodies do cleanly remove plaques and their precursor forms, but the cognitive benefit is only "30% slowing" of decline—not improvement—and temporary and limited. This gap has led researchers to revive shelved cholinergic drugs. Xanomeline, originally developed for schizophrenia (now marketed as Cobenfy), showed in early trials on Alzheimer's patients that it could improve cognition; it's being retested now.

12:25 Imaging data challenges where Alzheimer's begins
A recently graduated young scientist used MRI and PET data to challenge the conventional wisdom: does Alzheimer's really start in the entorhinal cortex? His research showed instead that nucleus basalis of Meynert (the cholinergic hub) degeneration predicts subsequent entorhinal changes, not the reverse. New tools like optogenetics let researchers for the first time observe these neurons in detail, refocusing the field on the overlooked deep-brain structures.

22:50 America's power grid bottleneck is policy, not engineering
Despite heavy investment, America has built high-voltage transmission lines and capacity very slowly over recent decades. Near-term consequences: surging data-center demand pushes up electricity prices. Long-term: harder transition to renewables and less resilience against extreme weather outages lasting days. Technology is not the bottleneck; incentives and policy design are.

26:54 Territorial monopolies lock in rules from the 1930s
In the 1920s–30s, multiple utilities duplicated lines in the same regions, inefficiently, while large areas had no power at all. States granted single companies exclusive supply rights for specific territories in exchange for giving up pricing power; the state approved cost recovery. This "territorial" governance model persists, but problems now exceed single-company jurisdictions. Utah solar reaching Las Vegas requires cross-state coordination no one company can deliver.

34:06 Direct current lets power lines hide underground
U.S. transmission relies on AC; long-distance DC was historically too expensive. Voltage source converter (VSC-HVDC) technology now makes DC economic in some cases. The advantage: cables bury underground along existing roads and rail corridors—the Champlain-Hudson line in New York runs directly under the Hudson River. This avoids seizing private land and sidesteps opposition to high-voltage towers, potentially speeding project completion.

43:22 Every patient carries a drug-response genetic variant
Among ~100,000 All of Us participants with whole-genome data, researchers tested 16 common drug-response genes; every patient carried at least one variant. Critically, roughly one-quarter were already taking drugs affected by their variants—not a rare edge case but a routine clinical issue. The study also uncovered 17,000 previously unreported variants in these genes, providing frequency data needed to decide which populations should be tested and when.

item.title: Anthropic is using AI to build AI, doubling its research speed
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-eightythousand-metr-发现-anthropic-用-ai-造-ai-速度已翻倍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-eightythousand-metr-发现-anthropic-用-ai-造-ai-速度已翻倍/
item.description: METR's investigation finds that roughly 80% of Anthropic's current research acceleration comes from using its own AI to conduct research, which is precisely the early sign of recursive self-improvement that observers have warned about for years.
item.content:encoded:
METR's investigation finds that roughly 80% of Anthropic's current research acceleration comes from using its own AI to conduct research, which is precisely the early sign of recursive self-improvement that observers have warned about for years.

An independent institution spent 11 weeks examining Anthropic's internal data to produce this report; its core conclusions and supporting evidence include concrete numbers that could change how you assess AI risk, making it worth hearing in full.

0:00 Anthropic's research speed has doubled year-on-year
After 11 weeks examining Anthropic's internal test scores, training data, and employee interviews, METR concluded that as of October, Anthropic's speed on quantifiable tasks had roughly doubled from a year prior, with a confidence interval of 1.3 to 3x. One piece of evidence: plotting all of the company's model test scores (including three unpublished internal models) on a timeline, the slope suddenly doubled from October last year. METR also ruled out increased compute as the main driver—while compute has indeed increased, it cannot explain this acceleration.

2:57 Two years' progress compressed: what doubling really means
By late 2023, Claude was just a chatbot that couldn't read images or browse the web; by late 2025, it could work independently for over 30 hours and build a complete Slack-like application without human intervention. That's two years of progress. Then just one year later, AI helped solve a math problem that had puzzled mathematicians for 87 years. This is what METR means by walking through two years of progress in one year.

4:00 80% of the acceleration comes from AI assisting its own research
After ruling out simple explanations like increased compute, hiring surges, new data, and research breakthroughs, METR's best guess is that roughly 80% of the current acceleration comes from Anthropic using its own AI to assist research. But in the public report, most of the reasoning around this figure and the most persuasive evidence have been redacted by Anthropic; METR admits this forces outsiders to rely more on their judgment.

4:48 Researcher testimony aligns with end-to-end automation metrics
Internal Anthropic researchers said that in certain areas AI has dramatically accelerated work; one researcher's exact words are quoted. While this type of anecdotal evidence alone isn't compelling, it aligns with the timeline: the acceleration appears to have begun in October 2025, precisely when Claude could write code continuously and independently for hours. Anthropic's own data shows that earlier this year, Claude barely conducted research end-to-end, but by August could complete roughly a quarter of it under human supervision.

6:19 No clear factor will break this cycle in the near term
AI building AI differs from other technologies: the stronger the AI, the faster it can help you build the next generation. This cycle only gets stuck at three bottlenecks—compute, training data, or algorithmic insights. METR examined all three and found no signs of constraint within the next year; they admit to low confidence and changing views with new information, but cannot rule out further acceleration in the next six months, or even acceleration of the acceleration itself.

7:33 Toby Ord's challenge and METR's response
Philosopher Toby Ord pointed out that the test score line might have another explanation: Mythos comes from a much larger training run, and large training runs typically deliver a one-time capability jump. Excluding that factor, the acceleration is only 1.4x rather than 2x. But AI safety researcher Buck Shlegeris responded that test scores were never METR's main basis for their conclusion—they're only the part of the report that wasn't redacted and that the public could see. The evidence that made METR more confident in doubling was what got deleted.

10:41 Anthropic admits it has crossed its own safety threshold
Anthropic drew its own line: AI accelerating research to walk through two years of progress in one year. Its August public report claimed the acceleration was "below 2x," but using Anthropic's private data, METR calculated 1.97x. Just before the author finished this episode, Anthropic admitted in its latest IPO filing that based on expectations for the next generation of models and current velocity, the company has already crossed the line it drew for itself—but only said it is evaluating the impact, not what it will do.

11:45 Companies won't constrain themselves; regulation must step in
The logic for why AI companies won't stop is clear: if we stop, competitors will continue, and they might be even less careful. New York State legislator Alex Bores called for Congress to pass legislation banning AI companies from fully automating their own research; this proposal has supporters from Bernie Sanders to Steve Bannon. METR also points out that whether they get invited into the company, what they can see, and what the report says are all decided by Anthropic—the company even tightened its redaction rules in the final week, forcing METR to redo work and delay publication.

item.title: Data centers became one of the biggest losers in America's midterm elections
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-sciencevs-数据中心成了美国中期选举最大输家之一/

item.description: Congress's approval power hasn't changed, but the execution layer has been infiltrated by political screening; even with Democrats controlling both chambers, they cannot shake Trump's actual control over science—voters ultimately decided based on electricity costs and noise from AI data centers.
item.content:encoded:
Congress's approval power hasn't changed, but the execution layer has been infiltrated by political screening; even with Democrats controlling both chambers, they cannot shake Trump's actual control over science—voters ultimately decided based on electricity costs and noise from AI data centers.

No explosive reversals, but it explains the specific mechanism of "funds uncut but unreachable" and the details of how data centers unexpectedly became an election issue—worth listening to.

4:12 Funding totals unchanged, but money's destination has shifted
One-and-a-half years ago, NIH already terminated over a thousand projects related to climate change, vaccine uptake, and health issues. American aid cuts are predicted to cause 25 million deaths over the next fifteen years. Now it's becoming more opaque: these cuts have been institutionalized as routine screening procedures.

5:17 Scientific approval isn't the final gate; politics comes next
Even after expert panels score a project as "scientific excellence," the funds must pass through political review by NIH leadership and even RFK Jr.'s office before release, ensuring alignment with government priorities. This screening targets keywords; research touching women's health, LGBTQ rights, or vaccines gets held up—timing that coincides with the recent spike in measles cases.

8:30 Officials claim no cuts, but entire research fields have disappeared
NIH and NSF distribute similar total amounts as before, letting administrators say "no cuts." But fields explicitly required by Congress to receive funding—like women's health and health disparities research—have had their money redirected elsewhere, making some research topics nearly impossible to pursue.

11:35 RFK Jr. remains one of the more popular cabinet members
Democratic candidate Annie Andrews publicly called RFK Jr. a "liar and conspiracy theorist" and pushed for impeachment. But Max notes that despite scientists' disdain, RFK Jr. is actually fairly popular among cabinet members, and he had ambitions to run for president in 2028—meaning he may not leave easily or be forced out.

12:35 Candidates weaponized MAHA's language against MAHA itself
Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed didn't attack RFK Jr.'s MAHA movement head-on. Instead he launched his own Baha campaign—Building a Healthier America—borrowing MAHA-style language about "removing toxins from food" but directing "toxins" specifically at pesticides with scientific evidence behind them, reframing the rhetoric through a scientific lens.

16:50 Majorities named AI data centers a key reason to vote
NBC exit polls found 56% of voters thought AI and data centers were a major or decisive factor in how they voted. Of over 40 ballot measures restricting data center construction, nearly all passed—interpreted as anger over rising electricity costs, noise, and water use, not necessarily opposition to AI itself.

17:55 Data centers have become symbols of giants crushing ordinary people
Many towns report having almost no say in data center decisions, with the process opaque and feeling like big tech crushing small people once again. Silicon Valley and Big Tech bet heavily on Republicans and Trump; as data center controversy builds, public distrust of their motives rises noticeably, especially in Texas where Elon Musk poured in large sums.

21:00 Democrats control Congress but cannot override vetoes or Senate rules
Even with Democrats controlling both chambers, Trump can veto bills, and Democrats lack the two-thirds majority in both houses to override. Non-budget bills must also clear the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold; budget bills require Trump's signature. This means even if Democrats wanted to double NSF funding, it would likely fail on Trump's desk.

item.title: AI shrinks development cycles, reviving genres studios abandoned
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-a16z-ai-让做游戏从十年压到两年-烂genre要迎来文艺复兴/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-a16z-ai-让做游戏从十年压到两年-烂genre要迎来文艺复兴/
item.description: GTA6 took twelve years. Two a16z partners argue AI can now compress game prototyping to weeks, letting studios fund niche genres and new IPs rather than sequels.
item.content:encoded:
GTA6 took twelve years. Two a16z partners argue AI can now compress game prototyping to weeks, letting studios fund niche genres and new IPs rather than sequels.

Two partners share firsthand experience making games with their kids to explain how AI is reshaping game development. The episode is not information-dense throughout, but includes concrete examples worth your time.

2:04 Direct engine control, not just instructions, is what changed game development
Jonathan Lai identifies a breakthrough from roughly a month ago: models can now directly manipulate Blender, Unreal, and Unity instead of just telling users what to do. This means someone with no game dev experience can use Astra to write a game design doc, generate concept art, model, rig, import to engine, add sound, and export a playable game. Astra can even screenshot itself for QA, spotting and fixing its own bugs. This accounts for why early prototypes on X were so surprisingly polished.

3:05 Long cycles explain why studios won't risk new IP or unfamiliar genres
Jonathan explains that if a AAA game costs a decade and hundreds of millions of dollars to produce, producers become extremely conservative—approving sequels over new IPs, proven genres like first-person shooters over experimental types. Call of Duty is up to around 20 entries. When AI cuts both timelines and budgets, studios will fund unproven teams and new IPs. This unlocks structural innovation in gaming, not just cost savings.

9:12 AI drops the barrier to game-making from professional teams to single creators
Jonathan contends that games are uniquely complex multidisciplinary products, requiring simultaneous expertise in coding, art, design, and audio—a far higher barrier than photography or video. AI fills the skill gaps a solo creator lacks, letting someone with just an idea and reference images iterate toward a prototype. He expects many will quit halfway through, but some will fall in love with game development, causing a surge in creator numbers in the industry.

18:31 Counter-Strike and League of Legends grew from mods, not original designs
Jonathan points to Counter-Strike as a Half-Life mod, League of Legends inspired by Dota (itself a Warcraft III mod), and Fortnite and PUBG both descended from Arma's battle royale mod—all became billion-dollar franchises. AI now lets any fan of an IP simply tell Astra: ‘make me a Ghost of Tsushima with a voxel building system.’ If it's fun, it could grow into a new genre the way those historical mods did.

22:44 Falling development costs will revive expensive, niche genres like RTS
Anish points to genres like RTS, traditionally expensive to produce with poor returns—no one has made a good iPad RTS despite everyone wanting one—now facing possible full revival as dev costs drop. He also mentions ‘profession simulators,’ an extremely niche category he loves. He recently played a Tokyo subway conductor simulator; these games were economically unfeasible before, but with costs now low, even a tiny player base like his can support profitability.

27:47 IP creators historically don't profit from mods made from their own work
Jonathan flags a structural problem: historically, IP creators rarely profit from mods of their own work—Dota's original developers made little from League of Legends, and Half-Life's developers probably didn't make much from Counter-Strike. Now if companies embrace AI-driven remixes, mods, and decompilation-recompilation, the business model is still unclear. Only Minecraft is an exception, having natively benefited from mod ecosystems.

35:50 The real opportunity is new mechanics, not faster versions of existing games
Jonathan frames current studio use of AI for concept art, design docs, and prototypes as the ‘first wave’ of adoption—now standard practice. He argues that the truly exciting ‘second wave’ is using AI to create entirely new game mechanics and genres that don't exist today, expanding the total gaming market rather than just making GTA6 faster and cheaper.

36:51 The ultimate MMO would adapt in real-time to each player's preferences
Anish describes his vision of the ‘never-ending game’: today's MMOs are linearly scripted—if the game wants you to go from beach to forest but you prefer the ocean, it has no way to adapt. An adaptive MMO built with world models could generate an entirely new quest line in real-time for ocean lovers—suddenly spawning pirates and naval combat. He likens this to the ‘mind game’ in Ender's Game that adjusts itself to match Ender's current thoughts, suggesting future games might achieve this in reality.

item.title: Drug development's constraint isn't strict approval but invisible preclinical toxicity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-nopriors-药物研发卡住的根源不是审批太严-而是临床前看不见毒性/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-nopriors-药物研发卡住的根源不是审批太严-而是临床前看不见毒性/
item.description: Isomorphic Labs's thesis: drug cost inflation stems from clinical failures caused by preclinical blindness to toxicity—rat testing predicts human toxicity with only ~30% accuracy.
item.content:encoded:
Isomorphic Labs's thesis: drug cost inflation stems from clinical failures caused by preclinical blindness to toxicity—rat testing predicts human toxicity with only ~30% accuracy.

The essential content clusters around the mid-episode discussion of toxicity prediction and combination therapy; the first two minutes on Max's background can be skipped.

5:23 Drug development's constraint isn't strict approval but invisible preclinical toxicity
Over decades, scientific papers increased tenfold to twentyfold and new drug modalities—antibodies, small molecules, proteins, peptides—proliferated, yet annual approvals remained flat. Development costs ballooned from millions to $1.5 billion, timelines stretched from 8–9 years to 15, and every metric worsened. Max attributes this to an industry still trapped in experience-driven trial-and-error: hypothesize a molecule, then iterate in the real world. But molecular and biological design spaces are high-dimensional and combinatorially explosive; empirical search only captures low-hanging fruit.

14:36 The goal is experimental-grade accuracy, not faster experiments
Isomorphic's north star isn't running wet experiments faster but moving drug design entirely to the computer. Max uses AlphaFold as the exemplar: structure prediction once required months or years of X-ray crystallography; if the model reaches experimental accuracy, real-world validation becomes unnecessary. Internal leaderboards mark an ‘experimental accuracy’ baseline; once crossed, wet experiments shift from ‘learning and iteration’ to ‘verification’, drastically reducing cycles in the physical world.

17:42 Clinical trials are where drug failure and costs concentrate
Unpacking the 15-year, $1.5 billion timeline: small-molecule discovery and in-vitro work occupy only 2–3 years and ~$50 million; the rest is clinical. Most failure modes—unexpected toxicity, off-target effects, or mechanisms that hit the target yet harm the body—only emerge when the drug reaches patients; animal models and in-vitro tests miss them entirely. Real gains in failure prevention come from understanding these failure modes before patient exposure.

18:46 Generate proprietary data instead of relying on public databases
Public and industry-wide data are mostly passive byproducts of historical collection, biased, and unfit for training general models demanding generalization. Isomorphic generates its own required data distributions instead of relying on existing large databases. Max noted this approach revealed ‘surprisingly impressive data scaling laws’ in model training.

20:53 Rat toxicity testing predicts human outcomes with only about 30% accuracy
Regulators mandate animal proof of safety before human use, yet toxicity frequently emerges once drugs enter patients. Max argues directly: rats aren't humans; this ‘gold standard’ predicts human clinical toxicity with about 30% accuracy—and he half-jokes that if his team's AI hit 30%, he'd ask engineers to ‘do better’. He advocates combining in-vitro experiments, AI models, and new tissue-mimicking techniques—organoids and organs-on-chip—to model human clinical toxicity directly, bypassing the five-to-six-decade-old, unreliable animal proxy.

29:21 Combination therapy fails at safety engineering, not biology
HIV and cancer treatments use cocktail approaches—tumors contain mutation spectra; single drugs prompt resistance; hitting multiple targets simultaneously prevents escape. But real-world combination therapy is rare. Max explains: existing molecules are often intrinsically toxic or damage the liver; multiple drugs generate harmful interactions. The constraint isn't biological understanding but molecular design precision—molecules lack the refinement and safety. Better-engineered, cleaner molecules unlock multi-target therapy against complex pathways.

32:17 Acceptable risk varies by disease; safety standards shouldn't be one-size-fits-all
When asked whether safety-focused regulation slows drug development, Max grants patient safety must remain central but notes risk tolerance is dynamic: COVID's pervasiveness and severity shifted social acceptance of expedited review; late-stage cancer with no alternatives and chronic low-risk disease demand vastly different risk tolerance. True progress means faster access to better treatments, not uniform safety thresholds across all disease contexts.

35:42 Extending lifespan isn't enough—drug development must also improve later-life quality
Beating cancer and heart disease still leaves aging itself—accumulated chronic problems: bone and muscle loss, post-fall immobility, compromised wellbeing and quality of life. Decades past 80 aren't inherently well-lived. Max emphasizes the industry must work both directions: treat discrete fatal diseases to extend lifespan, and tackle aging's root mechanisms to extend healthspan.

item.title: Food harbors 135,000 ‘dark matter’ molecules that science doesn't yet understand
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-thejoyofwhy-食物里还藏着13-5万种-暗物质-分子-科学还不知道它们在做什么/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-thejoyofwhy-食物里还藏着13-5万种-暗物质-分子-科学还不知道它们在做什么/
item.description: Network scientists have discovered that besides roughly 150 known nutritional components, food contains 135,000 unclassified molecules—they provide no energy but, like thousands of drugs, perform micro-level regulation inside cells.
item.content:encoded:
Network scientists have discovered that besides roughly 150 known nutritional components, food contains 135,000 unclassified molecules—they provide no energy but, like thousands of drugs, perform micro-level regulation inside cells.

One episode tracing thirty years of network science: from scale-free networks to preferential attachment to disease modules to the ‘dark matter of nutrition’—dense with information, and the latter half's medical and food cases especially worthwhile.

4:09 Everything derives meaning from connection, not from existing alone
Barabási argues science has long focused on dissecting parts while forgetting the whole—genes, neurons, and people have no meaning in isolation; function emerges only through mutual connection. Consciousness is what neurons collectively do; life is what genes and molecules collectively do; society is what people collectively do. Network science begins by mapping connections first, then asking why they exist this way, rather than studying isolated components.

14:36 Networks grow through winner-take-all mechanisms, not random chance
Traditional random graph theory assumed connections between nodes were purely determined by chance, predicting that node degrees would follow a bell curve. But actual data from the World Wide Web showed that 98% of web pages had only 1 to 5 links, while Google at the time had 800 million—a difference of several orders of magnitude. Barabási and collaborators discovered the cause: ‘preferential attachment’—when new nodes enter a network, they're more likely to connect to nodes already highly connected. This natural process creates hub nodes as networks grow, and the larger the network, the more extreme the gap between the largest hubs and smallest nodes becomes.

20:45 Random graph theory began as pure mathematics, not social reality
Strogatz explains that Erdős and Rényi originally posed the random network model to solve a pure mathematical question—using the metaphor of buttons and string: scatter buttons on a table, then randomly connect them with string. When the ratio of string to buttons reaches a critical point, picking up one button suddenly brings up a whole cluster—a discontinuous phase transition. They were pursuing the elegance of this phase transition proof, not simulating how real people make friends in society. This is the fundamental gap between the random model and actual networks.

24:57 Eighty-five percent of drugs never bind to the disease gene
Network medicine connects the ‘parts list’ from genomics with protein interactions to create a map. A disease's genes aren't randomly distributed in this network; they cluster in a specific ‘disease module’—like viewing a cell as a New York City map, psychiatric diseases clustered near Times Square, metabolic disease near Wall Street. Barabási's team found that 85% of drugs don't directly bind to the disease protein or gene itself, but instead act downstream.
